title: Animal body plans: comparing bodies to find out who is related

summary.text: A dolphin looks like a shark, but its flipper holds the bones of an arm and five fingers. What does that say about who is related? In this lesson you will survey the wrists of everyone at home, find leftover parts in your own body, and sort nine animals by what is inside.
summary.art: A dolphin and a shark swimming side by side, with the dolphin's flipper drawn see-through to show arm and finger bones, and the shark's fin drawn see-through to show thin straight rods.

intro.hook: Touch the tip of your thumb to the tip of your little finger. Now bend your wrist a little towards you. Does a thin cord stand up in the middle of your wrist? Some people have this cord and some people have none. Why would a body part be there in one person and missing in another?
intro.text: The cord is a tendon. A tendon is a tough string that joins a muscle to a bone. This one belongs to a small muscle in the forearm. People who have no such muscle grip just as strongly as people who have one. So why is the muscle there at all? The answer comes from comparing bodies. Orangutans climb with their arms, and they use this muscle fully. Humans share ancestors with orangutans, and those ancestors climbed. In this lesson you compare bodies the way scientists do. You survey the wrists in your family. You look for other leftover parts in a mirror. You also find out why a dolphin is a closer relative of a cow than of a shark.
intro.art: A child's forearm resting palm up on a table, thumb touching little finger, with a thin cord standing up in the middle of the wrist and a small arrow pointing to it.

outcomes: I can name five things scientists check to describe a body plan: cell layers, gut openings, body cavity, nerve cord and skeleton.
I can name the nine biggest groups of animals and say one feature of each body plan.
I can name the four main features of the chordate body plan and find traces of them in my own body.
I can explain the difference between homologous parts and analogous parts, and say which kind shows that animals are relatives.
I can say what a vestigial part is, find some in my own body, and explain why bodies have them.
I can run a fair survey of a body part that differs between people, and say what my results show.
I can explain how embryos, fossils and DNA are used together with anatomy, and what scientists do when they disagree.
I can explain, with an example, why a body is an altered older body and not a new design.

terms.meaning: The basic layout of an animal's body: which main parts there are and how they are arranged.
terms.example: A crow, a frog and you share one body plan: a head end, a backbone and four limbs.
terms.art: Outline drawings of a crow, a frog and a child, each with the backbone and four limbs marked in the same colour.

terms.meaning: One of the biggest groups of animals. All the animals in a phylum share one body plan. The plural is phyla.
terms.example: Ants, crabs and spiders are in one phylum, the arthropods.
terms.art: A large box labelled arthropods holding an ant, a crab and a spider, each with jointed legs.

terms.meaning: A very young animal who is just starting to form, before hatching or birth.
terms.example: Inside a hen's egg, the embryo is a small pale patch on the yolk in the first days.
terms.art: A hen's egg opened into a dish, with a tiny pale embryo and red blood vessels on the yolk.

terms.meaning: One of the first sheets of cells in an embryo. Each sheet goes on to build certain parts of the body.
terms.example: Your skin and nerves grew from the outer germ layer, and your muscles from the middle one.
terms.art: A ball-shaped embryo cut open to show three thin layers in three colours, labelled outer, middle and inner.

terms.meaning: The space or tube inside an animal where food is broken down and taken in.
terms.example: Your gut is a tube about eight metres long, from your mouth to your anus.
terms.art: An outline of a child with one long coiled tube drawn from the mouth to the bottom.

terms.meaning: The opening at the end of the gut, where waste leaves the body.
terms.example: An earthworm has a mouth at the front end and an anus at the back end.
terms.art: An earthworm drawn see-through, with a straight gut tube and labels at each end for mouth and anus.

terms.meaning: A space filled with liquid between the gut and the body wall. Scientists call it a coelom (say SEE-lome).
terms.example: Your heart, lungs and intestines hang in body cavities, so they can move without moving your skin.
terms.art: A cross-section of an earthworm drawn as two rings, an inner gut tube and an outer body wall, with a liquid-filled space between.

terms.meaning: The main bundle of nerves that runs along the body and carries signals between the brain and the rest.
terms.example: Your nerve cord is your spinal cord. It runs down your back inside your backbone.
terms.art: A child seen from behind with the spinal cord drawn as a pale line inside the backbone.

terms.meaning: A firm, bendy rod that runs along the back of every chordate embryo, under the nerve cord.
terms.example: You had a notochord before you were born. The soft discs between your backbones grew from what was left of it.
terms.art: A small fish-shaped embryo seen from the side, with a rod along the back in one colour and the nerve cord above it in another.

terms.meaning: An animal who has a notochord at some stage of life. Fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals are all chordates.
terms.example: A crow and a shark are both chordates. A crab is not.
terms.art: A crow, a shark and a child in a row, each with a line along the back, and a crab outside the row.

terms.meaning: The study of how the bodies of different animals are alike and different, part by part.
terms.example: Comparing a bat's wing with a human arm, bone by bone, is comparative anatomy.
terms.art: A bat's wing skeleton and a human arm skeleton side by side, with matching bones in matching colours.

terms.meaning: Parts of different animals that are the same part, inherited from a shared ancestor, even if they now do different jobs.
terms.example: Your arm and a whale's flipper are homologous. They hold the same bones in the same order.
terms.art: A human arm and a whale flipper with the upper arm bone, two forearm bones and finger bones coloured to match.

terms.meaning: Parts of different animals that do the same job but are built differently, and were not inherited from a shared ancestor.
terms.example: A butterfly's wing and a crow's wing are analogous. Both fly, but only the crow's wing has bones.
terms.art: A butterfly wing with a net of thin veins beside a crow's wing with bones and feathers.

terms.meaning: A part that has lost most or all of the job it did in the animal's ancestors.
terms.example: The small pink fold in the inner corner of your eye is vestigial. In a crow the same part is a full third eyelid.
terms.art: A close view of a human eye with an arrow to the small pink fold at the inner corner, beside a crow's eye half covered by a pale third eyelid.

terms.meaning: A tough string that joins a muscle to a bone, so that the muscle can pull the bone.
terms.example: The cords that move on the back of your hand when you wiggle your fingers are tendons.
terms.art: The back of a hand with the fingers spread, showing four cords running from the wrist to the fingers.

terms.meaning: A parent, grandparent, or anyone further back in the family line that an animal comes from.
terms.example: Dolphins and cows share ancestors who walked on four legs more than 50 million years ago.
terms.art: A family tree with a small four-legged animal at the bottom and a dolphin and a cow at the tips of two branches.

terms.meaning: The remains or the mark of a living being from long ago, kept in rock.
terms.example: Fossil bones of early whales have been found in Kutch in Gujarat.
terms.art: A slab of pale rock holding the dark fossil skull and leg bones of a four-legged animal.

terms.meaning: The long molecule inside every cell that carries the instructions for building a body. It is passed from parents to young.
terms.example: Scientists compared the DNA of whales and hippos and found them to be close relatives.
terms.art: A twisted ladder shape drawn large, with a small whale and a small hippo beside it.

terms.meaning: When animals who are not close relatives come to look alike over many generations, because they live in the same way.
terms.example: Sharks and dolphins both have a smooth, pointed shape for swimming fast.
terms.art: A shark and a dolphin drawn as two outlines, one on top of the other, almost matching.

explanations.concept: A body plan is set early, in the embryo
explanations.definition: A body plan is the basic layout of an animal's body. Its main features are set while the animal is still an embryo, a very young animal who is just starting to form.
explanations.description: You can see some of a body plan from outside: a ring or two matching sides, segments or none. Scientists also ask five questions about the inside. How many layers of cells does the embryo have? Does the gut have one opening or two? Is there a liquid-filled space round the gut? Where does the main nerve cord run? Where are the hard parts? Why do these features matter more than colour or size? Because they are decided very early in an embryo's life, and everything later is built on them. A change at such an early step would upset every later step. The usual explanation is that this is why body plans have stayed almost the same for hundreds of millions of years, while colour, size and shape have changed many times.
examples: A mouse and a blue whale differ hugely in size, but both embryos lay down a backbone, a skull and four limb buds in the same order.
An ant and a crab look different, but both are built in segments with a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs.
A builder can repaint a house easily. Moving the foundation means pulling the house down.
explanations.art: A row of three tiny embryos of a fish, a chick and a mouse that look much alike, with an arrow from each to a very different adult.

explanations.concept: Two layers of cells or three
explanations.definition: Germ layers are the first sheets of cells in an embryo. Jellyfish and their relatives have two germ layers. Most other animals have three.
explanations.description: Early in life, an embryo folds into sheets of cells. Heinz Christian Pander found three such sheets in chick embryos in 1817. Each sheet builds certain parts. In animals with a backbone, the outer layer makes the skin, the nerves and the brain. The inner layer makes the lining of the gut and the lungs. The middle layer makes muscle, bone, blood, the heart and the kidneys. A jellyfish embryo has only the outer and inner layers, with a jelly between them. Why does a third layer matter? It gives an animal thick muscles and solid organs between the skin and the gut. That makes fast swimming, digging and walking possible. This is a simplified picture. A jellyfish can still squeeze and swim, because some cells in her two layers can shorten the way muscle does. Sponges are different again. They have no germ layers at all.
examples: Your brain and your skin both grew from the outer layer, which is why both began at the surface of the embryo.
The muscle you eat in a piece of fish or chicken grew from the middle layer.
A jellyfish is mostly the jelly that lies between her two thin layers.
explanations.art: Two cut-open embryos side by side, one with two coloured layers and jelly between, labelled jellyfish, and one with three coloured layers, labelled frog.

explanations.concept: One gut opening or two: the sac and the tube
explanations.definition: A sac gut has one opening, which takes food in and lets waste out. A tube gut has two openings: a mouth where food enters and an anus where waste leaves.
explanations.description: A sea anemone, a jellyfish and a flatworm each have a gut shaped like a bag. Food goes in through the mouth. What is left over comes back out through the same mouth. An earthworm, a snail, an ant, a starfish and you have a gut shaped like a tube. Food travels one way. Why does this matter? In a tube, the animal can eat again while the last meal is still being digested. Also, every bite passes the same places in the same order. So each part of the tube can do one job well: grinding at the front, breaking food down in the middle, taking in water near the end. You test this with a sock and a paper tube in the experiment Sac or Tube. A sac is not a worse gut. Sea anemones and their relatives have lived well with one for more than 500 million years. A sac suits an animal who waits for a big meal and then rests.
examples: A sea anemone who has eaten a small fish pushes the bones back out through her mouth.
Your own gut has a mouth to grind, a stomach to churn and a long intestine to take food into the blood, in that order.
An earthworm eats soil at the front end while leaving worm casts from the back end.
explanations.art: A sea anemone cut open to show a bag-shaped gut with one opening, beside an earthworm cut open to show a straight tube with an opening at each end.

explanations.concept: The body cavity: a tube inside a tube
explanations.definition: A body cavity is a liquid-filled space between the gut and the body wall. Its scientific name is coelom.
explanations.description: Think of an earthworm as two tubes, one inside the other. The inner tube is the gut. The outer tube is the body wall, with its skin and muscles. Between them is a space filled with liquid. Why is the space useful? First, the gut can squeeze food along without the whole body having to move. Second, organs such as the heart have room to grow and to move. Third, the liquid cushions the organs from knocks. In a worm, the liquid also keeps the body firm, so that the muscles have something to push against. Your body has such spaces too. Your heart beats and your intestines churn all day, and your skin stays still, because they hang in liquid-lined cavities. A flatworm has no body cavity. The space between her gut and her skin is packed with cells. She also has no blood system, so every cell has to lie near the surface to get oxygen. That is why flatworms are thin and flat.
examples: After a meal your intestines squeeze and slide about, and you see nothing from outside.
When a cook cleans a fish, the gut lifts out easily, because it lies loose in the body cavity.
A flatworm is solid all the way through, like a folded dosa with no air inside.
explanations.art: A cross-section of an earthworm as two rings with liquid between, beside a cross-section of a flatworm drawn solid with a small branched gut.

explanations.concept: Which opening forms first: the mouth or the anus
explanations.definition: In an early embryo, a small dent forms and deepens into the gut. In starfish, fish, humans and their relatives, this first opening becomes the anus, and the mouth forms later.
explanations.description: An embryo starts as a hollow ball of cells. One side pushes inwards, as when you press a thumb into a soft ball. The dent becomes the gut. Its opening is the embryo's first opening. In starfish, sea urchins and all animals with a backbone, that first opening becomes the anus. The mouth breaks through later at the other end. Scientists call this group the deuterostomes, which means 'mouth second'. In snails, earthworms and insects, textbooks long said that the first opening becomes the mouth. That group is called the protostomes, 'mouth first'. This is a simplified picture. In some of the 'mouth first' animals, the first opening closes in the middle and gives both a mouth and an anus. Scientists now sort the two groups mainly by DNA. But the main point holds. A starfish begins life the way you did. So a starfish is a closer relative of yours than a snail or a bee is.
examples: A sea urchin embryo and a human embryo both make the anus first and the mouth second.
A starfish has no head and five arms, yet her embryo makes these two openings in the same order as a fish embryo.
An ant, a snail and an earthworm all belong to the other big group.
explanations.art: A hollow ball of cells with one side pushed in to form a pocket, shown in three steps, with the first opening labelled and a second opening breaking through at the far end.

explanations.concept: The nine biggest groups of animals
explanations.definition: A phylum is one of the biggest groups of animals, and every member shares one body plan. Scientists count about 30 phyla. Nine of them hold most of the animals you will ever meet.
explanations.description: Here are the nine, with roughly how many kinds have been named. Sponges, about 10,800: no tissues, no gut, a body full of holes. Cnidarians, about 16,000: jellyfish, corals and sea anemones, with two layers, a ring shape and a sac gut. Flatworms, about 29,500: three layers, two matching sides, a sac gut and no body cavity. Roundworms, about 25,000: a tube gut and a smooth body with no segments. Annelids, about 17,000: earthworms and leeches, with a tube gut, a body cavity and segments. Molluscs, about 85,000: snails, clams and octopuses, with a soft body and often a shell. Arthropods, about 1,257,000: insects, spiders and crabs, with segments, jointed legs and a skeleton on the outside. Echinoderms, about 7,500: starfish and sea urchins, with five-part bodies and the anus formed first. Chordates, more than 70,000: fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals, with a rod along the back. More than 1.5 million kinds of animals have been named so far. About four in every five of them are arthropods.
examples: In a city flat you can usually find arthropods (ants, flies, spiders), chordates (people, crows, geckos) and sometimes a mollusc (a snail after rain).
A bath loofah looks like a sponge, but it is the dried inside of a gourd, a plant.
Coral reefs in the Gulf of Mannar and in Lakshadweep are built by cnidarians.
explanations.art: Nine boxes in a row, each holding one animal: a sponge, a jellyfish, a flatworm, a roundworm, an earthworm, a snail, an ant, a starfish and a crow.

explanations.concept: The chordate body plan: four features you had before you were born
explanations.definition: Every chordate has four main features at some stage of life: a notochord, a hollow nerve cord along the back, openings or folds in the throat, and a tail that goes on past the anus.
explanations.description: A fish keeps all four features for life. You had all four as an embryo, and each one left a trace. The notochord is a firm, bendy rod along the back. Your backbone formed round yours, and what was left of the rod became part of the soft discs between your backbones. The hollow nerve cord became your spinal cord and brain. In the fourth week after you began, folds called pharyngeal arches formed in your throat. In a fish they hold up the gills. In you they became parts of the jaw, the three tiny bones of the middle ear and a small bone in the throat. You also had a tail. It showed most clearly when you were about 31 to 35 days old. It shrank, and its base is your tailbone. Chordates have a fifth feature too, a groove in the throat that became your thyroid gland. Why does every chordate share these? Because all chordates inherited them from the same ancestors.
examples: The lancelet, a small animal who lives in sea sand, keeps the notochord for life and never grows a backbone.
A sea squirt has the four features only as a swimming larva, the young form. The adult sits on a rock like a small bag.
The bones that carry sound through your ear grew from the same folds that hold up a fish's gills.
explanations.art: A small human embryo seen from the side, with four labels: the rod along the back, the nerve cord above it, the folds in the throat and the tail.

explanations.concept: Comparative anatomy: comparing bodies to find relatives
explanations.definition: Comparative anatomy is the study of how the bodies of different animals are alike and different, part by part. It is one of the main ways to find out which animals are relatives.
explanations.description: In 1555 the French traveller Pierre Belon drew a bird's skeleton beside a human skeleton and matched them bone for bone. In 1680 the English doctor Edward Tyson cut open a porpoise. He found a folded brain like the brains of four-legged land animals, and he placed the porpoise with them. That is the method. You look past the outside, which is shaped by how the animal lives. You compare the inside, part by part. Why does the inside tell you more? Because a way of life can change the outside quite fast. A swimmer becomes smooth and pointed, whoever her ancestors were. But the deep build of a body, such as which bones there are and how they join, is inherited and changes slowly. So when two animals share many detailed inside features that their way of life does not explain, the best explanation is that they inherited them from the same ancestors.
examples: A bat and a sparrow both fly, but a bat has fur, milk and four long finger bones in each wing. Those features put her with mice, not birds.
A caecilian of the Western Ghats looks like a big earthworm, but has a skull, teeth and a backbone. Caecilians are amphibians, like frogs.
A barnacle looks like a small shell on a rock, but the young swim on jointed legs. Barnacles are relatives of crabs.
explanations.art: An old-style drawing of a bird skeleton standing beside a human skeleton, with letters marking the matching bones.

explanations.concept: The same part, or the same job? Three checks
explanations.definition: Homologous parts are the same part in different animals, inherited from a shared ancestor. Analogous parts do the same job but were not inherited from a shared ancestor.
explanations.description: In 1843 the English anatomist Richard Owen gave the word homologue its meaning: 'the same organ in different animals under every variety of form and function'. How can you tell that two parts are the same part? Owen used three checks. Position: is the part in the same place, joined to the same neighbours? Make-up: is it built from the same pieces? Growth: does it form in the same way in the embryo? Your arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper pass all three. Each has one upper bone, then two bones, then many small bones, then finger bones. Each grows from a bud at the shoulder. A butterfly's wing fails all three. It has no bones, and it grows from the body wall. Here is a careful point. A bat's wing and a crow's wing are homologous as front limbs, because both inherited the limb. They are analogous as wings, because flying arose separately in bats and in birds. Only homologous parts show that animals are relatives.
examples: A mole's digging hand and a horse's front leg are homologous. The jobs differ and the bones match.
A dolphin's tail fin and a shark's tail fin are analogous. The dolphin's has no bones in the blades and beats up and down.
The spines of a cactus and the thorns of a rose both protect, but spines are changed leaves and rose thorns grow from the skin of the stem.
explanations.art: A human arm, a bat wing, a whale flipper and a mole's hand in a row with matching bones in matching colours, and a butterfly wing set apart with a cross-out of the word 'bones'.

explanations.concept: One pattern, used twice in you: your arm and your leg
explanations.definition: Serial homology means that one body uses the same pattern more than once, in parts that repeat along the body.
explanations.description: You do not need another animal to compare bodies. Compare your arm with your leg. The arm has one bone above the elbow, two below it, a cluster of small bones at the wrist, five bones in the palm, and finger bones. The leg has one bone above the knee, two below it, a cluster at the ankle, five bones in the sole, and toe bones. Your thumb has two bones and each finger has three. Your big toe has two and each other toe has three. Why would a hand and a foot match so closely, when one holds a pencil and the other is walked on? Because both grow from limb buds that follow the same instructions in the embryo. The body uses one pattern twice and then changes each copy to suit a job. You check this on yourself in the activity Your Leg Is a Second Arm.
examples: Your elbow bends forwards and your knee bends backwards, because the arm buds and leg buds turn opposite ways before birth.
The bones of your backbone repeat one pattern more than thirty times, changed a little from neck to hips.
A prawn's feelers, jaws, walking legs and swimming legs are one repeated limb, changed for each job.
explanations.art: A child's arm skeleton beside a leg skeleton, turned to line up, with the one bone, the two bones, the cluster and the five rays coloured to match.

explanations.definition: A vestigial part is a part that has lost most or all of the job it did in an animal's ancestors. Vestigial does not mean useless.
explanations.description: Look in a mirror at the inner corner of your eye. Beside the pink bump is a small pink fold. In crows, cats and crocodiles, that part is a full third eyelid that sweeps across the eye. In you only the fold is left. You have other leftovers. Three small muscles are joined to each ear. Most monkeys use theirs to turn the ears towards a sound. In people they do very little, though some people can wiggle their ears. Goosebumps are tiny muscles lifting your body hair. In a furry animal this traps warm air and makes the animal look bigger. Your tailbone is the base of a tail. The wrist muscle you look for in the Wrist Tendon Survey is missing in some people. Why are such parts still there? Because bodies are inherited. A part that is no longer needed is not removed at once. Over many generations it shrinks, and in some members of the family it is not built at all. Many leftover parts keep a smaller job. Your tailbone still anchors muscles.
examples: Pythons have two small spurs near the tail, the remains of hind legs. They are sometimes used in mating.
Fish who live in dark caves have eyes that no longer see.
An ostrich cannot fly, but uses her wings in displays and to keep cool.
explanations.art: A child looking closely into a hand mirror at the inner corner of one eye, with a small inset drawing of a crow's third eyelid half closed.

explanations.definition: Comparative embryology is the comparing of embryos. Young embryos of related animals look much more alike than the adults do.
explanations.description: A young fish embryo, a young chick embryo and a young human embryo look much more alike than the adults do. Each has a row of folds in the throat and a tail. As they grow, they become more and more different. Why are embryos useful to someone who compares bodies? Because they show parts that the adult has lost or changed past recognising. A starfish embryo shows two matching sides. A barnacle's young shows jointed legs. A human embryo shows a tail. In 1866 Ernst Haeckel went further. He said that an embryo replays the adult forms of the animal's ancestors, one after another, so a human embryo passes through a 'fish stage'. That turned out to be wrong, and his drawings made embryos look more alike than they are. A human embryo never has gills and is never a fish. What is true is simpler. Embryos of relatives resemble each other, because they are built by inherited steps, and the earliest steps are changed the least.
examples: The folds in a human embryo's throat never open into gill slits. They become parts of the jaw, ear and throat.
A dolphin embryo grows small hind limb buds, which then shrink away.
The tail of a human embryo shows most clearly at about five weeks, and then shrinks.
explanations.art: Three early embryos of a fish, a chick and a human drawn side by side and looking much alike, with the throat folds and the tail labelled on each.

explanations.concept: The same genes build very different bodies
explanations.definition: Many of the genes that lay out a body are shared by animals with very different body plans. A gene is one instruction in an animal's DNA.
explanations.description: A fly's eye is made of hundreds of tiny lenses. A mouse's eye has one lens, as yours has. For a long time scientists took these two eyes to be fully separate inventions. In 1995 Georg Halder, Patrick Callaerts and Walter Gehring switched on one gene, called eyeless, in the wrong parts of a growing fly. Extra eyes grew on the wings, the legs and the feelers. Mice have a matching gene, called Pax6. When the mouse gene was put into a fly, it also made eyes grow. They were fly eyes, not mouse eyes. So the gene does not hold the design of an eye. It works like a switch that says 'build an eye here', and each animal builds the eye of their own kind. Why does a fly's switch work like a mouse's? The best explanation is that both inherited it from one ancestor, more than 500 million years ago, who probably already used it for sensing light. Scientists call this deep homology: the parts look unrelated, and the instructions under them are shared.
examples: People born with a damaged Pax6 gene have eyes with no iris, the coloured ring.
The Hox genes mark out head, middle and tail in flies, mice and humans.
An octopus eye and a human eye arose separately, yet both use the Pax6 switch.
explanations.art: A fruit fly with a small extra red eye growing on one leg and another on a wing, beside a drawing of a mouse with an arrow from the mouse to the fly.

explanations.definition: DNA can be compared between animals, letter by letter, in the same way that bones are compared. Close relatives have more of their DNA in common.
explanations.description: Most of the time, bones and DNA tell the same story. Sometimes they disagree, and then scientists look for more evidence. Whales are the best example. Early whale fossils had teeth like those of an extinct group of wolf-like, hoofed meat-eaters. So for years those were taken to be the whale's ancestors. Then DNA put whales next to hippos, inside the group of even-toed hoofed animals such as cows, deer and pigs. Which was right? In 2001 two teams found early whales with legs in Pakistan. Their ankle bones had a double-pulley shape that only the even-toed hoofed animals have. The bones had agreed with the DNA all along. The right bone had not yet been found. DNA has also shown that termites are a branch of the cockroaches, and that falcons are closer to parrots than to kites and eagles. Why not use DNA alone? Because almost no fossil has any DNA left. For animals of the distant past, bones are all there is.
examples: Termites live in colonies as ants do, but a 2007 DNA study placed them inside the cockroach family tree.
A pangolin has armour like an armadillo, but DNA puts pangolins closest to cats, dogs and bears.
A swift looks like a swallow, but shares a very short, thick upper wing bone with hummingbirds.
explanations.art: A whale's small ankle bone with two rounded ends, like two pulleys, drawn beside the matching ankle bone of a deer, with a hippo and a whale behind.

explanations.concept: Is an insect built like us, but upside down?
explanations.definition: In an insect, the main nerve cord runs along the belly and the heart lies along the back. In an animal with a backbone it is the other way round.
explanations.description: In 1822 the French scientist Etienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire cut open a lobster and laid her on her back. In that position the order of her parts matched an animal with a backbone: nerve cord on top, gut in the middle, heart below. He said that all animals share one plan. In 1830 he argued this in public in Paris against Georges Cuvier, who said that body plans are separate and are shaped by what each animal needs. Most scientists of the time judged that Cuvier had won. In 1996 the question came back. Edward De Robertis and Yoshiki Sasai showed that the genes which decide 'back' and 'belly' in a fly embryo match those in a frog embryo, but work on opposite sides. You draw both layouts and turn one over in the activity The Upside-Down Test.
examples: When you peel a prawn, the dark line along the back is the gut, and the nerve cord is underneath on the belly side.
Your own nerve cord is at your back, inside the backbone, and your heart is towards your front.
In a fly embryo a signal on the back side stops nerves from forming there. In a frog embryo the matching signal works on the belly side.

perspectives.explanation: An ancestor of the chordates turned over, so that the old belly became the back. The matching genes on opposite sides are the evidence. The nerve cord of an insect and your spinal cord are then the same inherited part.

The shared ancestor may have had only a loose net of nerves all over the body. Each group then gathered the net into a cord on a different side. On this view nothing turned over, and the two nerve cords arose separately from shared genes.

explanations.concept: A body is an altered older body, not a new design
explanations.definition: Each kind of animal comes from earlier animals by small inherited changes. So every body is an older body that has been altered, and it keeps signs of the older one.
explanations.description: An engineer who needs a new machine can start with a blank sheet. Living bodies never do. Each generation can only alter what the parents passed on. In 1977 the French biologist Francois Jacob put it this way: evolution works like a tinkerer, someone who makes do with whatever is already at hand. The clearest sign is a part that takes a strange route. A nerve runs from your brain to your voice box. In a fish, the matching nerve goes straight to the gills, passing a blood vessel near the heart. In animals with necks, the heart sits lower in the chest. The nerve still loops under that blood vessel. So it runs down the neck, round the vessel and back up. In a giraffe this detour is about 4.6 metres long. Nobody planning a giraffe from a blank sheet would lay the nerve that way. It makes sense only as a fish's layout, stretched.
examples: Your food and your air cross paths in your throat, which is why people sometimes choke. Lungs began as a pouch off the gut.
A whale's flipper holds finger bones, though a whale never uses fingers.
A panda strips bamboo with a 'thumb' that is a wrist bone grown long, because her real thumb was already lined up with the other fingers.
explanations.art: A giraffe drawn see-through, with one nerve shown as a coloured line running from the head down the whole neck, round a blood vessel near the heart and back up to the throat.

explanations.concept: What counts as 'the same part'? Nobody has a complete answer
explanations.description: Comparative anatomy rests on one idea: two parts are the same part if they were inherited from one ancestor. Owen's three checks work well for bones. But the genes have brought puzzles. Sometimes two parts that are clearly the same part in two animals turn out to be built by partly different genes. Sometimes one gene, such as Pax6, helps to build parts that arose separately. So is 'sameness' in the bones, in the genes, or in how the embryo builds the part? Scientists and philosophers still argue about this. Most use all three kinds of evidence together and say plainly where they disagree.
examples: Insect wings may have grown from old leg parts, from the body wall, or from both. The evidence is still argued over.
The earliest four-limbed animals had more than five fingers. Acanthostega, who lived about 365 million years ago, had eight on each hand.
The three little bones in your ear match jaw and gill-arch parts in a fish. Are they still 'the same' bones?
explanations.art: A question mark made of three small drawings: a bone, a twisted DNA ladder and a tiny embryo.

agreed.text: The front limbs of all animals with a backbone and four limbs are built from the same bones in the same order.
agreed.evidence: Pierre Belon matched a bird's skeleton to a human skeleton bone for bone in 1555. Every skeleton studied since, from frogs to whales, fits the same pattern of one bone, two bones, small bones and finger bones.

agreed.text: Whales, dolphins and porpoises come from four-legged land mammals of the even-toed hoofed group. Hippos are their closest living relatives.
agreed.evidence: DNA places whales next to hippos. Early whales with legs, found in Pakistan in 2001, have the double-pulley ankle bone of that group. Indohyus, a fox-sized fossil animal from Kashmir, has the thick ear bone otherwise known only from whales.

agreed.text: Some healthy people have no palmaris longus muscle in one or both forearms, and their grip is just as strong.
agreed.evidence: A study of 385 young adults in Jabalpur in 2010 found the tendon missing on one side in about 17 in every 100 people, and on both sides in about 3 in every 100. Surgeons often remove this tendon to repair another, and the hand works as before.

agreed.text: A human embryo has folds in the throat and a tail, as a fish embryo has.
agreed.evidence: The folds, called pharyngeal arches, appear in the fourth week. The tail shows most clearly at 31 to 35 days and then shrinks. Both can be seen in embryos under a microscope.

agreed.text: A fly and a mouse use matching genes to start building an eye.
agreed.evidence: In 1995 Georg Halder, Patrick Callaerts and Walter Gehring switched on the gene in other parts of a fly, and extra eyes grew there. The matching mouse gene had the same effect in a fly.

agreed.text: Termites are a branch of the cockroaches.
agreed.evidence: A DNA study by Inward and colleagues in 2007 placed termites inside the cockroach family tree, next to wood-eating cockroaches.

challenging.claim: A whale is a kind of fish.
challenging.who: Most people in Europe until the 1700s. Carl Linnaeus listed whales as fish in 1735.
challenging.for: Whales live their whole lives in water and have fins and a fish-like shape.
challenging.against: Whales breathe air with lungs, feed their young on milk, and have arm and finger bones in the flippers. Linnaeus moved them to the mammals in 1758.
challenging.context: This claim sorts animals by where they live and how they look from outside.

challenging.claim: An embryo replays the adult forms of its ancestors, so a human embryo passes through a fish stage.
challenging.who: Ernst Haeckel, a German biologist, in 1866.
challenging.for: Human embryos do have throat folds and a tail, as fish embryos do.
challenging.against: The folds never become gills. Embryos resemble other embryos, not adult ancestors. Haeckel's drawings made the embryos look more alike than they are.
challenging.context: This idea was taught in schools for about a hundred years.

challenging.claim: A vestigial part is a useless part.
challenging.who: A common belief. In 1893 Robert Wiedersheim listed 86 parts of the human body as wholly or partly without a job.
challenging.for: People with no palmaris longus muscle lose no grip strength. Cave fish with blind eyes get no sight from them.
challenging.against: Many leftover parts keep a smaller job or gain a new one. The tailbone anchors muscles, and an ostrich uses her wings in displays. Jobs were later found for a number of the parts on old lists.
challenging.context: Vestigial means that a part has lost most of an older job. It does not mean that the part does nothing.

challenging.claim: An insect is laid out like an animal with a backbone, turned upside down.
challenging.who: Etienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, a French scientist, in 1822.
challenging.for: The genes that set 'back' and 'belly' in flies and frogs match, and work on opposite sides.
challenging.against: The shared ancestor may have had no single nerve cord at all. Then each group built a cord separately, and nothing was turned over.
challenging.context: Georges Cuvier argued against this in Paris in 1830, and for more than a century most scientists sided with Cuvier.

challenging.claim: Now that DNA can be read, comparing bones is no longer needed.
challenging.who: A view heard since DNA methods became cheap.
challenging.for: DNA corrected mistakes that anatomy had made about whales, termites, falcons and pangolins.
challenging.against: Almost no fossil has any DNA left, so extinct animals can only be placed by their bones. In whales, an ankle bone found later agreed with the DNA.
challenging.context: Today most scientists build family trees from DNA, bones and embryos together.

challenging.claim: The human body is the best-designed of all animal bodies.
challenging.who: A common belief, old and widespread.
challenging.for: Human hands and brains can do a very wide range of things.
challenging.against: Human bodies carry the same odd leftovers as other animals: a nerve that takes a detour, food and air paths that cross, a backbone that began as a level beam and now stands upright. Humans are one animal among many, altered from older animals in the same way.
challenging.context: Comparative anatomy treats the human body exactly as it treats any other body.

big_questions.q: Some people have the wrist tendon and some have none. Which of them has the 'normal' human body?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether 'normal' means the most common, the oldest, or the one that works. Do the three always agree?

big_questions.q: A bat's wing and your arm are the same part. A bat's wing and a butterfly's wing do the same job. Which pair is more alike?
big_questions.hint: It depends on what you mean by alike. Try answering once as a builder and once as a pilot.

big_questions.q: If your body holds parts from ancestors who climbed, swam and had tails, how much of your body is 'human'?
big_questions.hint: Look for a part of you that no other animal has in any form. It is harder than it sounds.

big_questions.q: Families, languages and tools also change bit by bit from older ones. Do they keep leftover parts too?
big_questions.hint: Think of the silent k in 'knife', or the buttons on a coat sleeve that open nothing.

big_questions.q: People sorted whales with fish for a very long time. What do we sort wrongly today because of how things look?
big_questions.hint: Think of things you group together because they look alike or are found in the same place.

big_questions.q: Body plans have hardly changed in 500 million years. Is that because they are the best possible, or because they are too hard to change?
big_questions.hint: Think about the builder who can repaint a house but cannot move the foundation.

big_questions.q: If no animal's body is a fresh design, is there any such thing as a 'perfect' animal?
big_questions.hint: Think about what perfect would be measured against, when every animal lives a different life.

story.title: The Zigzag Line
story.note: A made-up story. Yazhini, Kathir, Ammamma, her sisters and Saroja akka are imagined, and so is the mango with no stalk. These things are real: in a true Kanchipuram silk sari the body and the border are woven as separate cloths and locked together, the join is strong, and a zigzag line often marks where the body meets the end-piece, called the mundhi. Three shuttles are used, and a helper works one side of the loom.
text: The trunk had not been opened since before Yazhini was born. It stood under the stairs of Ammamma's house in Kanchipuram, and when the lid went up it let out a smell of camphor and old silk.

'Somewhere in there,' said Ammamma, 'are three pieces of my mother's wedding sari.' She knotted her keys back into the end of her own sari. 'She cut it in three when we were girls, one piece for each daughter. My sisters sent theirs back to me long ago, and I put them away with everything else. Now Malar is getting married. I want the three together again before the wedding.'
'What colour was it?' asked Kathir. He was seven, and he already had both arms in the trunk.
'Arakku. The red of lac. With a gold border of mangoes.' Ammamma picked up her cloth bag. 'I am going for flowers. Find them, and do not fight.'
The door closed. Kathir found it in two minutes.
'Here!' He held up a wide piece of silk, red as a new brick, with fat gold mangoes curling along the edge. 'Red. Gold. Mangoes. We are finished. Can we have the murukku now?'

Yazhini wanted to say yes. But all through the last holidays she had sat in the weaving shed two doors down, beside Saroja akka's loom. She had watched three shuttles fly, one from Saroja akka's hand and one from the hand of the helper on the far side. And Saroja akka had told her something, without once looking up from the threads.

'Anyone can make a cloth that looks like ours from the front, kanna. Turn it over. With us the border is its own cloth. It grows beside the body, and we lock the two together, thread by thread, as we go. Tear the sari and the border still holds. And where the body meets the mundhi, the two colours meet in a zigzag. That line is how you know.'

Yazhini turned Kathir's red silk over and held it against the window. The red threads ran straight on into the gold, from one edge of the cloth to the other. There was no join. There was no zigzag anywhere. It was one flat cloth, made in one go.
'This was made to look like one,' she said. 'It is not one.'
'But it is red and gold, and it has mangoes!'
'So does half of Gandhi Road. Help me take everything out.'

They emptied the trunk onto the mat. There were pillow covers and a baby's cap. There was a child's long skirt, a pavadai, in a blue so dark it was nearly black. There was a bag stitched from brown cloth worn as soft as a petal. There was a cradle cloth the colour of weak tea. Kathir pushed all of these to one side, because not one of them was red.

Yazhini picked up the dark pavadai, only because its hem felt heavy. She turned the hem up. On the inside, along the edge, ran a line of tiny locked loops. The border was its own cloth. She held it to the light. Under the dark dye she could just see the shapes woven into it. Mango, mango, mango, each with a small curled stalk.
'Someone dyed it,' she said slowly. 'Someone who did not like red.'
Kathir was not listening. He was counting with one finger. 'Four, five, six. Akka. This one has no stalk.'
She looked. The seventh mango was bare at the top, as if the weaver had missed one small step long ago and never noticed. Seven more along, there was another bare one. And seven after that.
There was something else. Just under the waistband, right across the skirt, the dark cloth changed its weave along a line of small sharp points. Up, down, up, down. A zigzag.
'A skirt does not need that,' said Yazhini. 'Only a sari has a mundhi. This was the end of a sari before it was ever a skirt.'

After that Kathir would not let her touch anything first. He unpicked one seam of the brown bag with a safety pin. Locked loops. He counted mangoes with his nose almost on the cloth. 'Seven. No stalk!' He shook out the cradle cloth and counted again, and shouted so loudly that the neighbour's dog barked.
Then, because he was a fair boy, he went back to his own bright red piece and counted its mangoes all the way round. Every one of them had a stalk.

When Ammamma came in with jasmine in her bag, the red silk lay folded on the stairs. On the mat, in a row, lay a nearly black skirt, a brown bag with one seam open and a cradle cloth the colour of tea.

'What is this? I said red.' Then she stopped. She put down the flowers and knelt, which she did not often do now. 'That pavadai. Kamala wore that. She would never wear red, not from the day she could talk.' She turned up the hem and ran her thumb along the locked edge, and for a while she said nothing at all.
'How did you know?' she asked at last. 'They do not even look like each other.'
'We turned them over,' said Kathir.

Ammamma laid the three pieces end to end, the way they must once have lain on the loom. The bag came first, then the cradle cloth, then the skirt with its zigzag at the far end. Yazhini counted along the border, across the first cut and across the second. The mango with no stalk came round every seventh time, and it did not miss once.
story.epiphany: The colour and the use of each piece had changed completely, so looking at the outside gave the wrong answer. The way the cloth was built had not changed: the locked border and the same small fault repeated in all three. The zigzag in the skirt had no job there. It was left over from the time the cloth was a sari, and it showed what the skirt had once been.
ask: Why can two things that came from the same beginning end up looking very different?
Why can two things with different beginnings end up looking the same?
Which tells you more about where a thing came from: what it does now, or how it is built? Why?
A fault that is copied again and again can be strong evidence. Why is a shared fault better evidence than a shared colour?
Name a part of something in your home that has no job now and is left over from an older use.

roots.context: In the Wrist Tendon Survey you looked for a muscle cord that some people have and some people lack. You also found a fold in your eye that is a full eyelid in a crow. Here we ask what these leftover parts tell us about what a body is.

deep_truth.truth: In the Wrist Tendon Survey you looked for a forearm muscle that some people have and some people lack. Hands with no such muscle grip just as strongly. Orangutans, who climb with their arms, still use theirs fully. So a body holds parts whose main job belonged to ancestors who lived differently. No body is made new for the life it leads now: each one is an older body, altered.
deep_truth.habit: We think of each animal as built for the way they live, part by part, the way a tool is made for a job. That mixes up what a part does now with why the part is there. Many parts are there because ancestors had them, and the present job came later or has almost gone.
deep_truth.evidence: Some wrists in the survey show the tendon and some may not, and studies find no loss of grip without it. The pink fold in your eye is a working third eyelid in a crow. A whale's flipper holds finger bones. In a giraffe, one nerve runs about 4.6 metres down the neck and back, on a route that is direct only in a fish.

three.who_am_i: Your body is a record of your ancestors. The fold in your eye, the bump at the end of your backbone and the cord in your wrist come from animals who lived long before any human did.
three.what_is_life: Life does not start again from nothing. Every living body was made by altering a body that already worked.
three.what_is_this_world: The animals around you are not separate inventions. A crow's wing, a dolphin's flipper and your arm are one limb, changed in three ways.

roots.thread: All animals alive today come from one group of small early animals. From that one beginning came many body plans: bodies in two layers and in three, guts with one opening and with two, skeletons inside and outside. Under these differences, the same instructions are still at work. A fly and a mouse use matching genes to start an eye, and a starfish makes her gut openings in the same order as you did. Many sages taught that one life takes many forms. Comparative anatomy shows a precise version of that. The many kinds of animals are one family, and each body still carries the marks of the family it came from.

teachings.teaching: The Tamil poet says that he has been born as grass, as a shrub, as a worm, as a tree, as many kinds of beast, as a bird, as a snake, as a stone and as a human. He has been through every kind of birth, among beings that move and beings that stay still, and he has grown tired.
teachings.link: The poem is about the soul's many births, not about bones. But it treats the worm, the bird and the human as stages of one traveller, not as strangers. Comparative anatomy finds its own version of this in the body: a worm's tube gut, the throat folds of a fish and a climber's wrist muscle, all in one human.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 18 ('Perfect Happiness'), in Burton Watson's translation (paraphrased)
teachings.teaching: The Chinese text says that 'the seeds of things have mysterious workings'. It describes a long chain in which one kind of living being turns into another, from water plants to insects and at last to leopards, horses and humans, who in time return to the same workings.
teachings.link: The details are not science. Leopards do not give rise to horses. But the idea is that each kind of living being comes out of an earlier kind, and that humans are inside the chain. Bones, embryos and DNA show the same thing in detail.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), chapter 13
teachings.teaching: Darwin asks: 'What can be more curious than that the hand of a man, formed for grasping, that of a mole for digging,' the leg of a horse, the paddle of a porpoise and the wing of a bat should all be built on one pattern, with the same bones in the same places?
teachings.link: Darwin's answer was that all five inherited the limb from one ancestor, and each kind then altered it. This is the main idea of this lesson, in the words of the scientist who first explained it.

science.text: All animals share ancestors. Matching bones, matching embryos and matching genes are the evidence, and they agree with each other.
Whether the nerve cord of an insect and your spinal cord are one inherited part, turned over, or two parts that arose separately.
Why animals have only about thirty body plans, and why no new one has appeared for about 500 million years.

other_view.who: Georges Cuvier, the leading anatomist in France in the early 1800s
other_view.view: Cuvier compared more animal bodies than anyone of his time. He held that each animal's parts are as they are because the animal's way of life requires them. On his view, parts that are alike show that needs are alike. They do not show shared ancestors, and he held that kinds of animals do not change into other kinds. Later evidence went against him on that. But his main point is still true and still used: the life an animal leads shapes every part of the body.

practice.title: Read your own hand
practice.say: Sit still and hold one hand open in front of you. Breathe slowly. Open and close the hand three times. Watch the cords move on the back of it. Now think of a bat's wing. It has the same bones as this hand, grown long. Think of a whale's flipper. The same bones are inside it, grown short and wide. Look at your hand again for five slow breaths. Ask yourself quietly how old this hand is.
practice.kid: Hold one hand open. Open and close it slowly three times. Watch the cords move. A bat's wing has these same bones. So does a whale's flipper. Look at your hand for five slow breaths. How old is this hand?

ask: If every part of your body came to you from ancestors, is there a part that is only yours?
Your hand, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper are the same limb. Where does one animal's story end and the next begin?
A leftover part has lost its old job. Does that make it less a part of you?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged, looking at her open hand, with a faint bat's wing and a faint whale's flipper drawn behind it at the same angle, the matching bones in the same colour.

games.title: Odd Cousin Out: which two are the true relatives?
games.context: In this game each card names three animals. Two of them are close relatives, and the third only looks or lives like one of them. You pick the odd cousin out, and the back of the card gives the clue from inside the body.

printables.title: 12 trio cards, with the two true relatives and the clue on the back

items.b: Odd one out: shark. Dolphin and cow breathe air with lungs and feed their young on milk. The dolphin's flipper holds arm and finger bones. The shark is a fish with gills.
Odd one out: sparrow. Bat and mouse have fur and feed their young on milk. A bat's wing is skin stretched over four long fingers. A sparrow's wing is feathers on a short, stiff hand.
Odd one out: ant. DNA shows that termites are a branch of the cockroaches. Ants are closer to wasps and bees. Termites and ants look alike because both live in large colonies.
Odd one out: limpet. A young barnacle swims on jointed legs, as a young crab does. The adult barnacle fixes to a rock and catches food with feathery legs. A limpet is a snail.
Odd one out: kite. DNA shows that falcons are closer to parrots and songbirds than to kites and eagles. Falcons and kites look alike because both hunt from the air.
Odd one out: earthworm. A caecilian is an amphibian with no legs who lives in soil, for example in the Western Ghats. They have a skull, teeth and a backbone. An earthworm has none of these.
Odd one out: ant. Spider and scorpion each have eight legs and no feelers. An ant has six legs and two feelers. All three are arthropods, but the spider and scorpion are closer.
Odd one out: jellyfish. Octopus and snail are molluscs. Both have three cell layers and a tube gut. A jellyfish has two cell layers and a sac gut with one opening.
Odd one out: swallow. Swift and hummingbird share a very short, thick upper wing bone and tiny feet. Swifts and swallows look alike because both catch insects in the air.
Odd one out: armadillo. DNA shows that the closest living relatives of pangolins are the meat-eaters, such as cats, dogs and bears. Pangolins and armadillos came to have armour separately.
Odd one out: shark. Dugongs and elephants are mammals who share ancestors, and scientists place them in one group. The dugong breathes air and feeds her calf on milk. The shark is a fish.

Odd one out: flying squirrel. Sugar glider and kangaroo are marsupials: the tiny newborn finishes growing in the mother's pouch. A flying squirrel is a rodent, like a rat. Gliding skin arose separately in the two.

printables.title: Score sheet for one player: twelve rounds

rules: Cut out the twelve cards. If you have no printer, write the three animals on one side of a slip and the answer on the other. Shuffle them and put them in a pile with the three animals facing up.
Each round, read out the three animals on the top card. Do not turn it over yet.
Each player decides which animal is the odd cousin out: the one who is not a close relative of the other two. Each player writes their choice, and one reason, on their score sheet.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. A right choice scores 1 point. A reason that is about the inside of the body, the young or the DNA scores 1 more point, even if the choice was wrong.
Play all twelve cards. The player with the most points wins. If two players tie, each names an animal trio of their own, and the other players judge the better one.
If you play alone, try to score 14 points or more out of 24.

setup.art: A pile of twelve small cards on a table, the top one reading 'Dolphin, shark, cow', with two score sheets and pencils beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the twelve cards. Put them in a pile with the three animals facing up.

setup.art: Two children each writing on a score sheet behind a cupped hand, with the top card of the pile between them.
setup.caption: 2. Read the three animals. Write your odd one out and your reason.

setup.art: A hand turning a card over to show the answer on the back, while a child marks a point on her sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score 1 for the right animal and 1 for a reason from inside the body.

flow.do: Cut out and shuffle the twelve cards. Give each player a score sheet. Read the rules aloud. Check that everyone knows what 'close relatives' means: animals who share recent ancestors.
flow.say: Two of the three animals on each card are close relatives. One only looks or lives like them. Find the odd cousin out, and give a reason.
flow.kid: Two animals on each card are close relatives. Find the odd one out. Give a reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Odd Cousin Out. You set up the cards and learn the rules.
flow.parent: Keep the cards face up in the pile so that nobody sees the backs. A reason such as 'both have milk' or 'both have a backbone' earns the extra point. A reason such as 'both fly' does not.

flow.do: Play cards 1 to 6. After each card, every player says their reason aloud before the card is turned over.
flow.say: Tell me your odd one out and your reason. Then we turn the card over.
flow.kid: Say your odd one out and your reason. Then turn the card over.
flow.context: In this step of Odd Cousin Out you play the first six cards and say your reason each time.

ask.q: What kind of clue fooled you, and what kind of clue gave the right answer?
good: I was fooled by animals that look alike or live in the same place.
The right clues were inside: bones, milk, how the young grow.
Sometimes only DNA could tell.

flow.do: Play cards 7 to 12 in the same way. Then add up the points.
flow.say: Six more cards. Think about the inside of each animal before you choose.
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Think about the inside before you choose.
flow.context: In this step of Odd Cousin Out you play the last six cards and add up the points.
flow.parent: Children often score more in the second half, once they stop trusting shape and home. Say so if you see it happen.

flow.do: Ask each player which card surprised them most. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Tell us why.
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Why were the look-alikes not close relatives?
flow.context: In this step of Odd Cousin Out you talk about why animals who look alike are often not close relatives.

check.q: A swift and a swallow look alike. What is the most likely reason?
options: Both catch insects in the air
They are the same kind of bird
One learned the shape from the other
check.why: Animals who live in the same way often come to look alike over many generations. This is convergent evolution. The bones inside a swift's wing match a hummingbird's. If you picked 'learned', remember that body shape is inherited and is not learned.

flow.think: Make a trio card of your own. Which two are the true relatives, and what clue from inside would prove it?

experiments.title: The Wrist Tendon Survey: does every human arm have the same parts?
experiments.context: In this survey you look at both wrists of everyone at home for one thin cord, the tendon of a small forearm muscle. You find out whether every human arm is built with the same parts.
experiments.question: Does every person have the same muscles in the forearm? Out of all the wrists you can test, how many show the thin cord in the middle?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Out of all the wrists you will test, how many will show the cord: all of them, most of them, or about half? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every wrist is tested in the same way: forearm resting on a table, palm up, thumb tip touching little finger tip, wrist bent a little towards the face. Every wrist is looked at in the same bright light. You agree what counts as 'yes' before you start: a sharp cord in the middle of the wrist. Two people look at each wrist, and the second is not told what the first decided. You test everyone at home, and you do not leave anyone out because their wrist looks ordinary. Left and right wrists are written down separately, because the cord can be missing on one side only.

materials.item: a table near a window, or under a bright lamp
people to test, at least three, counting yourself
the results table, drawn on paper, and a pencil
a phone for video calls to relatives or friends (if you can)
a hand mirror

experiments.safety: Bend the wrist only gently, and stop if it is uncomfortable. Nobody presses hard on another person's wrist. Ask each person before you test them, and let anyone say no.

schedule.what: Guess, learn the wrist test on yourself, test everyone at home and by video call, try the ear test, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each person. Under the table, write how many wrists had the cord, how many had none and how many you were not sure of. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Example: 16 wrists in one family and their relatives
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different, and you may find no wrist without a cord.

setup.art: A child's forearm resting palm up on a table by a window, with the tip of the thumb touching the tip of the little finger.
setup.caption: 1. Rest the forearm palm up. Touch thumb tip to little finger tip.

setup.art: The same forearm with the wrist bent a little towards the face and a thin cord standing up in the middle of the wrist, marked by an arrow.
setup.caption: 2. Bend the wrist a little towards you. Look in the middle for a sharp cord.

setup.art: A child looking closely at a grandmother's wrist on the table while a parent waits to look second, and a results table lies beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Test both wrists of everyone. A second person checks without being told.

setup.art: A child holding a phone on a video call, where an aunt is holding her bent wrist up to the camera.
setup.caption: 4. Add relatives or friends by video call. Then count the wrists.

flow.do: Read the question aloud. Count the people at home and the wrists you can test. Ask your child for a guess and a reason. Write both above the table.
flow.say: We will look at every wrist at home for one thin cord. Out of all those wrists, how many will show it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many wrists will show the cord? All of them? Say why you think so.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wrist Tendon Survey. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Do you think all people have exactly the same muscles? Why?
good: Yes, because everyone has the same body parts.
Mostly, but people differ in small ways, like height.
It might depend on how strong you are. We can check.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Do not say yet that some people have no cord.

flow.do: Your child rests one forearm on the table, palm up, in good light. They touch thumb tip to little finger tip. Then they bend the wrist a little towards the face. Look at the middle of the wrist, just below the palm. Then do the other wrist.
flow.say: Rest your arm palm up. Touch your thumb to your little finger. Now bend your wrist towards you a little. What do you see in the middle of your wrist?
flow.kid: Rest your arm palm up. Touch thumb to little finger. Bend your wrist a little. Look in the middle for a thin cord.
flow.context: In this step of the Wrist Tendon Survey you learn the wrist test on your own two wrists.
flow.parent: If the tendon is there, a thin, sharp cord stands up in the middle of the wrist. It feels like a tight string. A second, flatter cord often shows beside it, nearer the thumb. That one belongs to a different muscle, and everyone has it. Write 'yes' only for a sharp cord in the middle. If you see only the flatter cord nearer the thumb, write 'no'. If you cannot tell, write 'not sure'. Plump wrists are harder to read, so look from the side as well.

flow.do: Test every person at home in the same way, in the same light. Check the left wrist and the right wrist. Your child looks first and decides. Then a second person looks and decides, without being told. Write yes, no or not sure for each wrist.
flow.say: Now we test everyone, the same way each time. You decide first. Then I will look, and we will see if we agree.
flow.kid: Test everyone at home, both wrists. Do it the same way each time. Write yes, no or not sure.
flow.context: In this step of the Wrist Tendon Survey you test both wrists of every person at home.

check.q: Why does a second person look at each wrist without being told the first answer?
options: So one person's mistake cannot settle the result
So the survey goes faster
Because the cord moves between looks
check.why: A cord can be hard to see, and a person who hopes for a result may see what they hope for. If two people decide separately and agree, the answer is more likely to be right. If you picked 'faster', notice that a second look takes more time. It is worth it.

flow.parent: Where the two checkers disagree, write 'not sure'. Do not argue it into a yes or a no.

flow.do: Call two or three relatives or friends on a video call. Ask each one to do the test and hold the bent wrist near the camera. Add them to the table. If no call is possible, go on with the people you have.
flow.say: A few people is a small group. Who can we call to add more wrists? Tell them exactly how to do the test.
flow.kid: Call a relative or friend. Tell them how to do the test. Add their wrists to the table.
flow.context: In this step of the Wrist Tendon Survey you add more people by video call, so the group is bigger.
flow.parent: Let your child give the instructions. Explaining the test clearly to someone else is part of doing it fairly. A wrist on a small screen is harder to read, so use 'not sure' freely.

flow.do: Now each person tries to move their ears without touching them. Each gets three tries. A watcher looks from the side, or the person uses the mirror. A moving scalp or eyebrow does not count. Write yes or no.
flow.say: Moving the ears is another part that some people have and some do not. Try to move your ears without touching them. I will watch from the side. Only the ear itself counts.
flow.kid: Try to move your ears without touching them. Three tries each. Write yes or no.
flow.context: In this step of the Wrist Tendon Survey you check a second body part that differs between people: the ear muscles.
flow.parent: Most people cannot move their ears, and some can. Everyone has the three small muscles behind and above each ear.

flow.do: Count the wrists with a cord, with none, and not sure. Count the people who can move their ears. Compare the counts with the guess. Your child writes three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Read the parent note aloud only after that.
flow.say: Count the yes wrists and the no wrists. Was your guess right? Why might a body part be there in some people and missing in others?
flow.kid: Count the wrists with a cord and without. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Wrist Tendon Survey show.

ask.q: What did you find, and did it match your guess?
good: Most wrists had the cord, but not all.
Every wrist we tested had one, but we tested only a few.
One person had it on one side only.

ask.q: People with no cord grip just as strongly. So why do some people have this muscle at all?
good: Maybe it was more useful long ago.
Maybe our ancestors used their arms differently.
Maybe other animals use it more than we do.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. The cord is the tendon of a muscle called palmaris longus. It helps a little in bending the wrist. Studies find that people with no such muscle grip just as strongly. Surgeons often borrow this tendon to repair another one. Orangutans, who climb with their arms, use the muscle fully. Humans come from ancestors who climbed. In humans the muscle has shrunk, and in some people it is not built at all. A part like this is called vestigial. The ear muscles are the same kind of leftover. Most monkeys turn their ears towards a sound. If every wrist in your survey had the cord, say so plainly. In studies in India, the cord was missing in roughly 1 in 15 to 1 in 5 of the hands or people checked. So a small group often has none missing.
flow.think: A dolphin's flipper holds finger bones that the dolphin never uses as fingers. How is that like the cord in a wrist?

experiments.title: Sac or Tube: which gut can eat while it digests?
experiments.context: In this test a sock stands for a gut with one opening, like a sea anemone's. A paper tube stands for a gut with two openings, like yours. You time how long each takes to 'digest' twelve paper balls, to find out which gut is faster and by how much.
experiments.question: A sock has one opening and a tube has two. Which one gets twelve balls of 'food' digested sooner, and about how many times as fast?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Which will finish twelve balls sooner, the sock or the tube? About how many times as fast? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both guts get the same twelve paper balls. In both, a ball counts as digested only when it has stayed inside for a slow count of ten. The same person counts aloud at the same speed, one count each second, using the seconds on a timer. The same person moves the balls. With the sock, balls go in and come out through the one opening only. With the tube, balls go in at one end and come out at the other. Only the kind of gut changes.

materials.item: a long sock
a sheet of newspaper and sticky tape, for the tube
sheets of scrap paper, crumpled into balls about the size of a lemon
a pen, to number the balls 1 to 12
a timer that shows seconds, such as a phone
a ruler, to push the last balls out of the tube

schedule.what: Guess, make the tube and the balls, time the sock twice and the tube once, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Write the seconds for each run in the table. Under the table, write how many times as fast the tube was as your best sock run. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Example: seconds to digest 12 balls

data.label: Sock, one ball at a time

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper rolled into a wide tube and taped, lying beside a long sock and twelve numbered balls of crumpled paper.
setup.caption: 1. Roll and tape a newspaper tube that holds five balls in a row. Number twelve paper balls.

setup.art: A child pushing a numbered paper ball into the open end of a sock while a parent watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. The sock: balls go in and out by one opening. Each must stay in for a count of ten.

setup.art: A child pushing a paper ball into one end of a paper tube held level, as another ball drops out of the far end onto the table.
setup.caption: 3. The tube: push one ball in at the mouth end on every second count.

setup.art: A paper tube with three bands drawn round it, labelled grind, break down and take in, with numbered paper balls lined up after it in order.
setup.caption: 4. Compare the times. Point to three places on the tube and see what every ball passed.

flow.do: Show the sock and say that it stands for a gut with one opening. Say that the tube you will make stands for a gut with two. Give the rule: a ball is digested only after a slow count of ten inside. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: A sea anemone's gut is a bag like this sock. Yours is a tube. Which will finish twelve balls sooner? How many times as fast? Why?
flow.kid: The sock is a gut with one opening. The tube has two. Guess which is faster.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sac or Tube. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Which will be faster, and why?
good: The tube, because food can keep moving along.
The sock, because it is wider and holds more.
They will be the same, because each ball waits for ten counts either way.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Many children expect no difference, because the count of ten is the same for both.

flow.do: Crumple twelve paper balls, each about the size of a lemon. Number them 1 to 12. Roll the newspaper into a tube a little wider than a ball and tape it. Trim the tube so that it holds exactly five balls in a row.
flow.say: Make twelve paper balls and number them. Now roll a tube that the balls can slide through. It must hold five balls and no more.
flow.kid: Make twelve paper balls and number them. Roll a tube that holds five balls.
flow.context: In this step of Sac or Tube you make the twelve food balls and the paper tube.
flow.parent: The tube must hold five balls, so that each ball spends ten counts inside. If the balls stick, roll the tube a little wider.

flow.do: Start with the sock. Your child may use any plan they like. Start the timer. Count aloud, one count each second. Stop when all twelve balls have been in for ten counts and are out again. Write the seconds and the plan.
flow.say: Here is the sock. Every ball must stay inside for ten counts. They go in and out through the top only. Use any plan you like. Go.
flow.kid: Digest twelve balls in the sock. Each stays in for ten counts. Use any plan.
flow.context: In this step of Sac or Tube you time the sock, using your own plan.
flow.parent: Do not suggest a plan. Most children start with one ball at a time. If they pull a ball out before its count of ten, it goes back in, and you mark one in the last column.

flow.do: Ask what slowed the sock down. Let your child think of a faster plan and run the sock again. Time it and write it.
flow.say: What slowed you down? Can you think of a faster plan for the same sock? Try it.
flow.kid: What slowed the sock down? Think of a faster plan. Try again.
flow.context: In this step of Sac or Tube you run the sock again with a better plan.

ask.q: With several balls in the sock, which one comes out first?
good: The last one that went in, because it is on top.
The first one in is at the bottom, so I must take the others out to reach it.
So new food comes out before it is ready.

flow.parent: The fastest plan is to put in several balls, wait for the last one to finish its count, and then empty the sock. While the sock is being emptied, it cannot take in food.

flow.do: Now the tube. Hold it level over the table. Start the timer. Your child pushes one ball in at the mouth end on every second count. From the sixth ball, each push sends the oldest ball out at the far end. Push the last five out with the ruler, one on every second count. Write the seconds.
flow.say: Now the tube. Push one ball in at this end on every second count. Watch what happens at the other end.
flow.kid: Push one ball into the tube on every second count. Watch the far end.
flow.context: In this step of Sac or Tube you time the paper tube, which has two openings.
flow.parent: Check that the balls come out in the order 1, 2, 3. Each one has been inside for five pushes, which is ten counts.

flow.do: Compare the three times. Your child works out how many times as fast the tube was as the best sock run. Then point to three places along the tube and name them grind, break down and take in. Your child writes what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at the three times. How many times as fast was the tube? Why? And what did every ball pass on its way through the tube?
flow.kid: Compare the times. Why was the tube faster? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of Sac or Tube show.

check.q: Why can a tube gut have one part for grinding and another for taking food in?
options: Every bite passes the parts in the same order
A tube is longer than a sac
Tube guts belong to bigger animals
check.why: In a tube, food moves one way, so every bite meets the grinding part first and the taking-in part later. In a sac, new food and old waste share one space, so the parts cannot be set out in order. If you picked 'longer', remember that a short tube still works this way.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. The tube could take in a new ball while five others were still inside, and the oldest ball always left first. In the sock, the oldest ball was at the bottom, so new food had to wait or be taken out again. Counted on paper, one ball at a time takes about 170 counts, five at a time about 80, and the tube about 35. A sea anemone lives well with a sac.
