She eats a big meal now and then, and rests while she digests.
flow.think: A sea anemone sits still and waits for food. An earthworm eats all night long. Which gut suits which life?

activities.title: Three Leftovers in the Mirror
activities.context: In this activity you use a mirror to find out that your body still carries three parts that do a bigger job in other animals: a fold in the eye, the tiny muscles under your hairs and the muscles round your ears.

materials.item: a hand mirror, or a wall mirror in good light
an ice cube in a tumbler

activities.record: Draw your eye with the pink fold in the inner corner, or tell your grown-up where it is. Write the three leftovers you looked for and one thing you wonder about each.

setup.art: A child holding a hand mirror close to her face near a window, looking at the inner corner of one eye.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the inner corner of your eye. Find the small pink fold beside the pink bump.

setup.art: A child holding an ice cube against the back of her neck with one hand and looking at the raised hairs on her other forearm.
setup.caption: 2. Hold ice on the back of your neck for ten seconds. Watch the hairs on your arm.

setup.art: A child looking sideways into a mirror and trying to move one ear, with a parent watching from the side.
setup.caption: 3. Try to move your ears without touching them.

flow.do: Your child looks in the mirror at the inner corner of one eye, the corner nearest the nose. There is a small pink bump. Just beside it, on the white of the eye, is a thin pink fold. Ask what they notice and what they wonder.
flow.say: Look at the corner of your eye, next to your nose. Find the pink bump. Now find the thin fold beside it. What do you notice? What might it be for?
flow.kid: Look at the corner of your eye, near your nose. Find the thin pink fold. What might it be for?
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Leftovers in the Mirror. You find a fold in the corner of your eye.

ask.q: What do you notice about the fold, and what do you wonder?
good: It does not move when I blink.
It looks like the edge of something.
Do other animals have one?

flow.parent: Let your child guess first. Then say that crows, cats and crocodiles have a third eyelid in that corner. It sweeps across the eye to clean and protect it. In humans only this fold is left. If a crow or a pigeon sits at your window, watch them blink. A pale film sometimes flicks across the eye.

flow.do: Your child holds the ice cube against the back of the neck for ten seconds and watches one forearm. Look for small bumps and for hairs standing up. If none come, ask when they last had goosebumps.
flow.say: Hold the ice on the back of your neck and watch your arm. What happens to the hairs? What use could that be to an animal with thick fur?
flow.kid: Hold ice on the back of your neck. Watch your arm hairs. What happens?
flow.context: In this step of Three Leftovers in the Mirror you look for goosebumps, and ask what they are for.

ask.q: What use could standing hairs be to a furry animal?
good: Fluffed-up fur keeps more warm air in.
A cat looks bigger when her fur stands up.
We have so little hair that it hardly helps us.

flow.parent: Each body hair has a tiny muscle at its root. When the muscle pulls, the hair stands up and the skin makes a bump. Goosebumps do not always come with ice, so do not force it. A cold bath, a fright or a favourite song can also bring them.

flow.do: Your child tries to move their ears without touching them, watching in the mirror. Then ask which of the three leftovers might be missing altogether in some people. Write the guess down for the Wrist Tendon Survey.
flow.say: Try to move your ears. Now think about the fold, the goosebumps and the ear muscles. Could a part like these be missing altogether in some people?
flow.kid: Try to move your ears. Could a leftover part be missing in some people? Guess.
flow.context: In this step of Three Leftovers in the Mirror you try your ear muscles, and guess whether leftover parts can be missing.

check.q: What is the best explanation for the pink fold in the corner of a human eye?
options: It is left over from a third eyelid
It grew because people rub their eyes
It is a new part, still growing
check.why: Many other animals with a backbone have a full third eyelid in the same place. Humans share ancestors with them, and in humans only the fold is left. If you picked 'rubbing', remember that something you do to your body is not passed on to your children.

flow.think: If a part has lost its old job, what might happen to it over thousands of generations?

activities.title: Nested Boxes: sort nine animals by what is inside
activities.context: In this activity you sort nine animals, one from each of the nine biggest groups. First you sort them by how they look. Then you sort them by four features of the inside, and the boxes you draw turn into a family tree.

materials.item: plain paper
a pencil
small slips of paper, for the animal names

activities.record: Keep the sheet with the four nested boxes. Under it, write which two of the nine animals are the closest relatives of each other on your sheet, and how you can tell.

setup.art: Nine slips of paper on a table, each with one name: sponge, jellyfish, flatworm, roundworm, earthworm, snail, ant, starfish, crow.
setup.caption: 1. Write nine animal names on nine slips.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a large box drawn on it holding eight slips, and the sponge slip lying outside the box.
setup.caption: 2. Clue by clue, draw a box round the animals who share the feature.

setup.art: A sheet with four boxes drawn one inside another, the smallest holding only the starfish slip and the crow slip.
setup.caption: 3. Read the boxes. The smaller the box two animals share, the closer they are.

flow.do: Write the nine names on slips: sponge, jellyfish, flatworm, roundworm, earthworm, snail, ant, starfish, crow. Ask your child to sort them into groups by how they look. Ask for the reason for each group. Keep a note of the groups.
flow.say: Here are nine animals. Put the ones that look alike together. Tell me why you made each group.
flow.kid: Sort the nine animals by how they look. Say why you made each group.
flow.context: This is the first step of Nested Boxes. You sort nine animals by how they look from outside.
flow.parent: Most children put the three worms together, and the starfish with the jellyfish. Say nothing yet.

flow.do: Lay all nine slips on a sheet. Read out one clue at a time. For each, your child draws a box round the animals who have that feature. Clue 1: tissues and a gut. All but the sponge. Clue 2: three layers of cells in the embryo. All in box 1 but the jellyfish. Clue 3: a gut with two openings. All in box 2 but the flatworm. Clue 4: the embryo's first opening becomes the anus. Only the starfish and the crow.
flow.say: Now sort by the inside. I will read four clues. For each one, draw a box round the animals who have that feature.
flow.kid: Listen to each clue. Draw a box round the animals with that feature. Or ring them with string.
flow.context: In this step of Nested Boxes you sort the nine animals by four features of the inside.
flow.parent: Each new box sits inside the one before. Box 3 still holds six animals: roundworm, earthworm, snail, ant, starfish and crow. Box 4 holds two. Four clues are far too few to sort the others. Scientists use hundreds of features, and DNA as well.

flow.do: Compare the boxes with the first sort. Ask where the three worms ended up, and where the starfish is. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at your first groups and at the boxes. Where did the three worms go? Who is the starfish with now? What does a small shared box tell you?
flow.kid: Where did the three worms go? Who is the starfish with now?
flow.context: In this step of Nested Boxes you compare sorting by looks with sorting by the inside.

check.q: On your sheet, which pair shares the smallest box?
options: Starfish and crow
Starfish and jellyfish
Flatworm and earthworm
check.why: The starfish and the crow are alone together in box 4, because both make the anus first as embryos. Animals who share a small box share more inherited features, so they are closer relatives. If you picked the jellyfish, you sorted by the ring shape, which arose separately in the two.

flow.parent: A long thin body with no legs suits burrowing and sliding, so it has arisen many times. The three worms belong to three different phyla.
flow.think: The roundworm, earthworm, snail and ant are still in one box. What extra clue could split them?

activities.title: The Upside-Down Test: is a prawn laid out like a fish, turned over?
activities.context: In this activity you find out why some scientists think a prawn is a fish turned upside down. You show where the nerve cord, the gut and the heart lie in each, then flip one and compare. Scientists have argued about this since 1822.

materials.item: small sheets of plain paper
a pencil and three colour pencils: blue, yellow and red

activities.record: Keep the fish drawing. On the back, write the prawn's colour order from top to bottom. Then write one sentence for the idea that the plan was turned over and one sentence for the other explanation.

setup.art: A simple side-view drawing of a fish with three stripes along the body: blue on top, yellow in the middle, red below.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a fish from the side: nerve cord on top in blue, gut in yellow, heart below in red.

setup.art: A simple side-view drawing of a prawn with three stripes along the body: red on top, yellow in the middle, blue below.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the pencils in a row for a prawn: heart on top in red, gut in yellow, nerve cord below in blue.

setup.art: A child's hands turning the prawn drawing upside down and holding it next to the fish drawing, so the stripes match.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the pencil row upside down. Compare the order of the colours with the fish.

flow.do: Your child runs a hand down the bumps of their own backbone. The nerve cord is inside those bones. Then they put a hand on the chest, where the heart is. On the first sheet they draw a fish from the side with three stripes: blue for the nerve cord on top, yellow for the gut in the middle, red for the heart below. A child who would rather not draw tells you the colours and you draw.
flow.say: Feel your backbone. Your main nerve cord runs inside it, along your back. Your heart is at your front. A fish is laid out the same way. Draw it.
flow.kid: Feel your backbone. Your nerve cord is inside. Draw a fish: blue on top, yellow, then red. Or tell your grown-up what to draw.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Upside-Down Test. You draw where three parts lie in a fish, and in you.
flow.parent: Blue is the nerve cord, yellow the gut and red the heart with its main blood vessel. The drawing is a simple map, not a true picture.

flow.do: Beside the fish drawing, your child lays the three pencils in a row for a prawn: red on top, yellow in the middle, blue below. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: In a prawn, an ant or an earthworm, the heart runs along the back and the nerve cord along the belly. Lay the pencils like that: red on top, yellow in the middle, blue below. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Lay the pencils for a prawn: red on top, yellow, then blue below.
flow.context: In this step of the Upside-Down Test you draw where the same three parts lie in a prawn.

ask.q: What do you notice when you look at the two rows?
good: The same three parts are in both.
The order is the other way up.
The gut is in the middle in both.

flow.do: Your child turns the pencil row upside down, so red is at the bottom, and compares it with the fish drawing. Ask what could explain the match. Then ask what does not fit: both mouths open on the belly side. After the flip, are the two bellies on the same side?
flow.say: Turn the pencil row upside down. What do you see now? What could explain it? A prawn's mouth and a fish's mouth both open on the belly side. After the flip, are the two bellies on the same side?
flow.kid: Turn the pencil row upside down. Do the colours match the fish now? Where is the belly of each?
flow.context: In this step of the Upside-Down Test you turn the prawn drawing over and look for what fits and what does not.

ask.q: What could explain why the order matches when one is turned over?
good: Maybe an ancestor of the fish turned over long ago.
Maybe it is chance, since there are only a few ways to stack three parts.
Maybe each built a nerve cord separately, on different sides.

flow.parent: Both explanations in your child's answers are held by scientists today. The genes that mark 'back' and 'belly' in flies and frogs match, and work on opposite sides, which supports a turn. But the mouth is on the belly side in both animals. If the body turned over, the mouth must have moved, and nobody is sure how.
flow.think: Three parts can be stacked in only six orders. How much should a matching order count as evidence?

activities.title: Your Leg Is a Second Arm: one pattern, used twice
activities.context: In this activity you count the bones of your arm and hand by feeling them. Then you guess the bones of your leg and foot, and check. You find that one body uses the same pattern twice.

materials.item: plain paper and a pencil

activities.record: Make two columns, one for the arm and one for the leg. In each, write the bones you found from top to bottom: one, two, a cluster, five in a row, and the number in each finger or toe.

setup.art: A child holding her own upper arm with the other hand, then her forearm near the wrist, with labels 'one bone' and 'two bones'.
setup.caption: 1. Feel your arm: one bone above the elbow, two below, then the small bones of the wrist.

setup.art: A child bending one finger and counting its three parts, and bending the thumb and counting two.
setup.caption: 2. Count the bones in each finger and in the thumb.

setup.art: A child sitting on the floor holding her shin with one hand and bending her big toe with the other.
setup.caption: 3. Guess the pattern in your leg and foot. Then feel and count.

flow.do: Your child grips the upper arm and feels one bone. Then they hold the forearm near the wrist and turn the palm up and down. Two bones move, one rolling over the other. Then they bend each finger and the thumb, and count the straight parts between the bends.
flow.say: Feel your upper arm. How many bones? Now hold your forearm and turn your palm over. How many? Now count the parts of a finger, and of your thumb.
flow.kid: Feel your upper arm, then your forearm. Count the bones. Count the parts of a finger and a thumb.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Leg Is a Second Arm. You count the bones of your arm and hand.
flow.parent: The answers are one bone, then two, then a cluster of eight small bones in the wrist, five long bones in the palm, three in each finger and two in the thumb.

flow.do: Do not touch the leg yet. Ask your child to guess the leg bones from top to bottom. Ask how many bones are in the big toe. Write the guess. Then they feel the thigh, the shin, the ankle and the toes, and count.
flow.say: Now guess your leg, from the top down. How many bones in the thigh? Below the knee? In your big toe? Why do you think so? Now feel and count.
flow.kid: Guess the bones of your leg, from the top down. Then feel and count.
flow.context: In this step of Your Leg Is a Second Arm you guess the bones of your leg and foot, then check.

ask.q: How many bones did you guess for the big toe, and why?
good: Two, like the thumb, if the foot copies the hand.
Three, like the other toes.
I did not know toes had separate bones.

flow.parent: The thigh has one bone. Below the knee there are two. The shin bone is at the front, and the lower end of the thinner one is the bump on the outside of the ankle. The ankle has a cluster of seven bones, and the sole has five long ones. The big toe has two bones and each other toe has three, though the small toes are hard to count.

flow.do: Compare the two columns. Ask what is the same and what is different. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at your two lists. What is the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Compare your arm list and your leg list. What is the same? What is different?
flow.context: In this step of Your Leg Is a Second Arm you compare the two limbs and ask why they match.

check.q: Why do your hand and your foot have the same pattern of bones?
options: Both grow from limb buds that follow the same instructions
Feet were once used as hands
Bones always come in these numbers
check.why: In the embryo, arms and legs start as four small buds, and each bud follows the same building steps. The body then alters each copy for a job. If you picked 'bones always come in these numbers', look at your backbone or your ribs. Their numbers are quite different.

flow.parent: Differences worth finding: the knee has a kneecap and the elbow has none. The forearm can twist and the shin cannot. The knee and the elbow bend in opposite directions.
flow.think: A horse walks on one toe on each foot. Which of your bones do you think a horse still has, and which has she lost?

activities.title: The Wing on the Plate: find your arm in a chicken wing (if your family cooks chicken)
activities.context: In this activity you take a cooked chicken wing apart and lay out the bones. You find the same pattern as in your own arm. If your family does not cook chicken, watch a pigeon or a crow stretch a wing instead, and find the elbow and the wrist.

materials.item: a whole cooked chicken wing, with all three sections, cooled
a plate and a sheet of paper
a pencil

activities.safety: Use a wing that is fully cooked and has cooled. A grown-up pulls the bones apart, because small bones can be sharp. Wash hands with soap afterwards. Put the bones in the bin, out of reach of pets, because cooked chicken bones can hurt a dog or a cat.
activities.record: Lay the bones on the paper in order. Beside each bone, write which part of your own arm it matches. Take a photo, or draw round the bones if you like.

setup.art: A whole cooked chicken wing on a plate, bent at its two joints into a Z shape, with a child's bent arm held beside it in the same shape.
setup.caption: 1. Bend the wing at its two joints. Hold your own arm beside it in the same shape.

setup.art: The bones of a chicken wing laid out in order on a sheet of paper: one thick bone, then two thinner bones side by side, then a small pointed group.
setup.caption: 2. Take off the meat. Lay the bones out in order: one, then two, then the hand.

setup.art: A child's drawing of the wing bones beside a drawing of human arm bones, with lines joining the matching bones.
setup.caption: 3. Hold each wing bone against your arm. Write beside it the part it matches.

flow.do: Put the whole wing on the plate. Your child bends it gently at its two joints. Ask which joint is the elbow and which is the wrist, and which section matches the upper arm. Write the guesses.
flow.say: This was a hen's wing. Bend it gently. It has two joints. Which is the elbow? Which is the wrist? Hold your arm beside it and tell me why.
flow.kid: Bend the wing at its two joints. Which is the elbow? Which is the wrist? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wing on the Plate. You bend the wing and guess which part matches which part of your arm.

ask.q: Which section of the wing matches your upper arm, and how can you tell?
good: The thick one that joined the body.
It has one joint at each end, like my upper arm.
I am not sure. We can look at the bones.

flow.do: A grown-up pulls the three sections apart and takes off the meat. Lay the bones on the paper in order. The thick section has one bone. The middle section has two, one thinner than the other. The tip has a few small bones joined together, with a small point at its base.
flow.say: I will take the bones out, and you lay them in order. How many bones in the first part? In the second? What does the tip look like?
flow.kid: Lay the bones in order. Count the bones in each part of the wing.
flow.context: In this step of the Wing on the Plate you lay out the bones of the wing and count them.
flow.parent: The first bone matches your upper arm bone. The two in the middle match your two forearm bones. The tip is the hand. A bird's hand has three fingers, and most of their bones are joined into one stiff piece that carries the long flight feathers. The small point at the base of the tip is the thumb.

flow.do: Your child holds each wing bone against their own arm, next to the bone it matches, and points. They lay the wing bones on the paper and write beside each one the part of their arm it matches: upper arm, forearm or hand. Then ask what the hen's ancestors might have used this limb for.
flow.say: Hold each wing bone against your own arm and point to the bone it matches. A wing even has a small thumb. What might the hen's ancestors have used this limb for?
flow.kid: Hold each wing bone against your arm. Point to its match. Write its name beside it.
flow.context: In this step of the Wing on the Plate you match the wing bones to your own arm bones.

check.q: A hen's wing has one bone, then two, then a small hand. What is the best explanation?
options: Birds and humans inherited the limb from shared ancestors
This is the only way to build a wing
Hens once used their wings as hands
check.why: The same order of bones is found in frogs, lizards, bats and whales, whatever the limb is used for. So the pattern is inherited. It is not the only way to build a wing, because a butterfly flies with no bones at all.

flow.think: A bat's wing is skin stretched over long fingers. A bird's wing is feathers on a short stiff hand. Which bones would you look at to tell them apart?

projects.title: The Family Leftover Map: three leftovers across three generations
projects.context: In this project you draw your family tree and find out, for as many relatives as you can, three things: whether each wrist shows the tendon cord, whether they can move their ears, and how many wisdom teeth the grown-ups have had. You look for whether these features run in the family.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, such as chart paper or the back of a calendar page
a pencil and two colour pencils
a phone, for calls and video calls to relatives

projects.safety: Ask each relative whether they are happy to take part, and accept a no. Some people do not like questions about their teeth or their body.

schedule.what: Draw the family tree with three generations and at least twelve people. Write your guess.
Test or call the first six people. Mark the tree.
Call the rest. Mark the tree.
Look for patterns, and write your claim, your evidence and what you are not sure of.

projects.record: On the tree, beside each person, write how many of their two wrists show the cord: 0, 1 or 2. Write E beside anyone who can move their ears. Beside each grown-up write the number of wisdom teeth, from 0 to 4, or a question mark. On day 4, write one claim, the evidence and one thing that could have misled you.

setup.art: A child drawing a family tree on a large sheet of paper, with grandparents at the top, parents and aunts and uncles in the middle, and children at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your family tree: three generations, twelve people or more.

setup.art: A child on a video call with a grandfather who is holding his bent wrist up to the camera.
setup.caption: 2. Test each person's wrists and ears. Ask the grown-ups about wisdom teeth.

setup.art: A finished family tree with two small wrist marks beside each name, some coloured in and some empty, and a letter E beside a few names.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the tree. Look for features that run along the family lines.

flow.do: Your child draws a family tree, or arranges one paper slip for each person. Include grandparents, parents, aunts, uncles, cousins, brothers and sisters. Aim for twelve people or more. Ask for a guess: will a missing cord or moving ears turn up in people who are closely related? Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Draw everyone you can reach. Do you think a missing wrist cord runs in families, like the shape of a nose? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make your family tree. Do missing cords run in families? Guess, and say why.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Family Leftover Map. You draw the tree and write your guess.
flow.parent: Include relatives by marriage too, but mark them, because they do not share ancestors with your child's side.

flow.do: Test the people at home, then call three or four relatives. Each one does the wrist test on both sides and tries to move their ears. Ask each grown-up how many wisdom teeth have come through or been taken out. Mark the tree after each person.
flow.say: Tell each person exactly how to do the wrist test: palm up, thumb to little finger, bend the wrist, look for a thin cord. Then ask about ears. Then ask the grown-ups about their wisdom teeth.
flow.kid: Test each person's wrists and ears. Ask grown-ups about wisdom teeth. Mark the tree.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Family Leftover Map. You test the first six people and mark the tree.
flow.parent: Wisdom teeth are the last four back teeth. They usually come through after the age of seventeen, and in some people one or more never form. Many grown-ups will not be sure of their number. Write a question mark for them.

flow.do: Call the remaining relatives and mark the tree in the same way.
flow.say: Who is still missing from the tree? Call them, and test them in exactly the same way as the others.
flow.kid: Call the relatives who are still missing. Test them the same way. Mark the tree.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Family Leftover Map. You finish testing and marking.
flow.parent: A wrist on a small screen is hard to read. Write 'not sure' beside it and leave the mark empty with a dot.

flow.do: Look at the finished tree together. Ask whether any feature turns up in a parent and a child, or in brothers and sisters. Your child writes a claim, the evidence and one doubt. Then read the parent note aloud.
flow.say: Look along the lines of the tree. Does anything turn up in a parent and their child? How sure can you be, with this many people?
flow.kid: Look for features shared by parents and children. Write your claim, your evidence and one doubt.
flow.context: This is day 4 of the Family Leftover Map. You look for patterns and say how sure you are.

ask.q: What would make you more sure of your claim?
good: More people in the tree.
Seeing the same feature in a parent and several children.
Testing another family to compare.

flow.parent: A missing cord is much more common in some parts of the world than in others, which suggests that genes play a part. How it is passed on has not been fully worked out. A tree of twelve people can hint at a pattern, but it cannot prove one. That is a fair thing for your child to write.
flow.think: If fewer and fewer people are born with this muscle, what might a wrist look like in a hundred thousand years?

challenges.title: Old Hand, New Job: turn a five-finger hand into a wing
challenges.context: In this challenge you start with a cardboard hand with five fingers and alter it into a wing that moves as much air as possible. You may only change what is already there, which is how bodies change over generations.
challenges.problem: A cardboard hand with spread fingers moves very little air when you fan with it. Alter the hand so that one sweep sends a ball of tissue paper as far as possible across a table. You must keep all five fingers.
constraints: Start from a tracing of your own spread hand, cut from thin cardboard.
Keep all five fingers. You may make a finger longer, shorter or wider, and you may join fingers with 'skin'. You may not add a sixth finger or a new part that does not grow from the hand.
Test each design in the same way: one sweep, three tries, without touching the ball.
Measure how far the ball rolls each time, and use the middle one of the three distances.

materials.item: thin cardboard, such as an empty cereal or biscuit box
scissors and sticky tape
broomsticks from a coconut-leaf broom, straws or ice-cream sticks, to lengthen fingers
a thin plastic carry bag or a sheet of newspaper, for skin
a ball of tissue paper the size of a lemon
a ruler or a measuring tape

challenges.safety: A grown-up helps with cutting cardboard. Broomsticks have sharp ends, so tape over the tips and keep them away from eyes.
general: Tape skin between all five fingers, as in a frog's foot.
Make the fingers much longer with sticks and stretch skin between them, as in a bat's wing.
Tape the fingers together into one wide, stiff paddle, as in a whale's flipper.
creative: Make only one finger very long, and stretch skin from that finger back to the wrist. Flying reptiles called pterosaurs did this with the fourth finger.
Join the fingers into a short, stiff hand and tape long paper strips along it as feathers. Birds did this.
Leave the thumb free and small, so that the wing can still hook onto things. Bats keep a clawed thumb.
Make the skin loose in one design and tight in another, and test which moves more air.
challenges.your_turn: Now alter a fresh five-finger hand for a different job: digging in soil, or paddling in water. Say which fingers you changed, what you had to give up, and which real animal's limb your design is most like.

setup.art: A child tracing round her spread hand on a piece of thin cardboard with a pencil, with scissors beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Trace your spread hand on cardboard and cut it out. Make two.

setup.art: A tissue-paper ball on a start line drawn on a table, with a cardboard hand held upright a little behind it, about to sweep.
setup.caption: 2. Put the tissue ball on a start line. Fan once from behind. Measure how far it rolls.

setup.art: A cardboard hand with thin sticks taped along the fingers to make them long, and a piece of plastic bag taped between the fingers like a bat's wing.
setup.caption: 3. Alter the second hand: lengthen, join or widen the fingers. Test it the same way.

flow.do: Your child traces their spread hand twice on cardboard and cuts both out, with help. Mark a start line on a smooth table and put the tissue ball on it. Hold the plain hand upright, a hand's width behind the ball. Sweep once towards the ball without touching it. Measure the roll. Do it three times.
flow.say: First we test a plain hand. One sweep, no touching. How far does the ball roll? Do it three times and keep the middle distance.
flow.kid: Cut out two cardboard hands. Fan the ball with a plain one. Measure three tries.
flow.context: This is the first step of Old Hand, New Job. You test how much air a plain cardboard hand moves.
flow.parent: The plain hand usually moves the ball only a few centimetres, because air slips between the fingers. Use the same sweep each time, as well as you can.

flow.do: Read the rule aloud: keep all five fingers, and only alter what is there. Ask your child how they could change the hand to move more air. Let them sketch or describe two ideas before they build.
flow.say: You may make fingers longer, shorter or wider, and you may add skin between them. You may not add new parts. What will you change, and why?
flow.kid: Keep all five fingers. Change only what is there. Sketch two ideas, or tell them to your grown-up.
flow.context: In this step of Old Hand, New Job you plan how to alter the hand without adding new parts.

ask.q: Why did the plain hand move so little air, and what would fix that?
good: The air went through the gaps between the fingers.
Skin between the fingers would close the gaps.
Longer fingers would make a bigger surface.

flow.do: Your child builds one design on the second hand with sticks, tape and skin. Test it three times in the same way and write the distances. If there is time, alter it once more and test again.
flow.say: Build your design. Then test it exactly as before: one sweep, three tries. Write each distance down.
flow.kid: Build your design. Test it three times, the same way as before. Write the distances.
flow.context: In this step of Old Hand, New Job you build your altered hand and test it.
flow.parent: A webbed hand usually sends the ball several times as far as the plain one. Very long fingers with loose skin can flop, which is a useful thing to find out.

flow.do: Compare the middle distances. Read out the usual solutions and the creative ones. Ask which real animal's limb the design is most like. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: How much farther did your design send the ball? Which animal's limb is it most like? What did your hand give up to become a wing?
flow.kid: How much farther did the ball go? Which animal's limb is your design like?
flow.context: In this step of Old Hand, New Job you compare your design with the wings and paddles of real animals.

check.q: A bat's wing and a whale's flipper are both altered five-finger hands. What does that show?
options: New limbs come from changing an old limb
Bats and whales both needed hands
Five is the best number of fingers for every job
check.why: Neither animal got a new kind of limb. Each has the inherited hand, with the fingers made long in the bat and short and wide in the whale. If you picked 'five is best', notice that a horse walks on one toe and a bird's wing has three fingers. The number can shrink, but the pattern is still the old one.

flow.think: Your design can fan air, but can it still hold a pencil? What does a bat give up by having wings for hands?

items.p: A dolphin's flipper and your arm hold the same bones in the same order. What are such parts called?
items.why: Homologous parts are the same part, inherited from a shared ancestor, even when the jobs differ. Analogous parts share a job and not a build. Vestigial parts have lost most of an old job.

items.p: Which pair of wings does the same job with a different build?
items.why: A butterfly's wing has no bones and a crow's wing has arm bones, so the two are analogous. The other two pairs hold the same bones, so they are homologous.

items.p: A vestigial part is always a useless part.
items.why: False. Vestigial means that a part has lost most of the job it did in ancestors. Many such parts keep a smaller job. Your tailbone still anchors muscles.

items.p: An animal who has a notochord at some stage of life is called a ____.
items.why: The notochord is the firm rod along the back of the embryo. Fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals are all chordates.

items.p: Match each body plan feature to an animal who has it.
pairs: Skeleton on the outside and jointed legs
Rod along the back of the embryo
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A sea anemone is a cnidarian, an ant is an arthropod, a starfish is an echinoderm and a crow is a chordate. Each group has a body plan of their own.

items.p: Sort each part: is it homologous to your arm, or not?
items.a: as given
items.why: The bat, the whale and the horse inherited the same limb bones that you did. A butterfly's wing and an octopus's arm have no bones and arose separately.

items.p: In a wrist survey, why are the left and right wrists written down separately?
opts: The cord can be missing on one side
items.why: Some people have the tendon in one forearm and not in the other. Counting people instead of wrists would hide that.

items.p: A jellyfish embryo has two layers of cells, and a frog embryo has three.
items.why: True. The frog's middle layer builds muscle, bone and blood. A jellyfish has only the outer and inner layers, with jelly between.

items.p: Explain why a sea anemone has to finish one meal before starting the next big one.
items.a: A sea anemone's gut is a sac with one opening. Waste has to leave through the mouth, so the sac must be emptied before new food goes in.
items.why: A strong answer says that the gut has one opening, and that food and waste use the same way in and out.

items.p: Draw your arm bones from shoulder to fingertips. Label one bone, two bones, wrist bones and finger bones.
items.a: A drawing with one upper arm bone, two forearm bones side by side, a cluster of small wrist bones, five palm bones and the finger bones.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the order: one, two, a cluster, five in a row, then fingers. This is the order found in every limb of this kind.

items.p: Draw a young embryo from the side. Label the notochord, the nerve cord, the throat folds and the tail.
items.a: The nerve cord runs along the back. The notochord lies just under it. The throat folds are below the head. The tail goes on past the anus.
items.why: These are the four main features of the chordate body plan. A human embryo has all four.

items.p: The small pink fold in the corner of your eye is left over from a third ____.
items.why: Crows, cats and crocodiles have a full third eyelid in that corner. In humans only the fold is left.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shoulder to the fingertip.
items.why: This order is the same in your arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a frog's front leg.

items.p: A thumb has 2 bones and each finger has 3. How many thumb and finger bones are in one hand?
items.why: Four fingers with 3 bones each make 12. The thumb adds 2. 12 and 2 make 14. A foot has the same count: 2 in the big toe and 3 in each other toe.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Ant. Crab. Spider. Snail.
items.a: Snail. The other three are arthropods, with jointed legs and a skeleton on the outside. A snail is a mollusc.
items.why: Ants, crabs and spiders share one body plan. A snail has a soft body with no jointed legs.

items.p: A caecilian looks like a big earthworm but has a skull, teeth and a backbone. Who are their closer relatives?
items.why: Caecilians are amphibians with no legs. A skull, teeth and a backbone are inherited features that earthworms do not have. The long shape suits life in soil and has arisen many times.

items.p: Early whales with legs had a double-pulley ankle bone. What did that bone show?
opts: Whales belong with the even-toed hoofed animals
Whales are close relatives of sharks
items.why: Only even-toed hoofed animals, such as cows, deer and hippos, have that ankle bone. Swimming does not need it, so it is an inherited mark.

items.p: A fly's eye-starting gene and a mouse's match. What is the best explanation?
opts: Both inherited the gene from one ancestor
Flies and mice eat the same food
The two eyes are built alike
items.why: The eyes themselves are built very differently. A matching gene is best explained by a shared ancestor who already had it.

items.p: A human embryo is, for a short time, a fish.
items.why: False. A human embryo has throat folds and a tail, as a fish embryo has. But the folds never become gills. Embryos of relatives resemble each other. They do not turn into each other's adults.

items.p: Termites are closer relatives of cockroaches than of ants.
items.why: True. DNA places termites inside the cockroach family tree. Termites and ants look alike because both live in large colonies.

items.p: Animals who are not close relatives but come to look alike show ____ evolution.
items.why: Convergent evolution happens when animals live in the same way. Sharks and dolphins both became smooth and pointed for fast swimming.

items.p: Match each leftover part in humans to the working part in another animal.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each human part is in the same place and is built the same way as the working part in the other animal. In humans it has lost most of that job.

items.p: Sort each animal by gut: one opening, or two?
items.a: as given
items.why: Cnidarians and flatworms have a sac gut. Annelids, molluscs and chordates have a tube gut with a mouth and an anus.

items.p: Put these steps in the making of an embryo's gut in order.
a: A hollow ball of cells forms
One side of the ball pushes inwards
The dent deepens into a gut
A second opening breaks through at the far end
items.why: The dent gives the first opening. In starfish and in animals with a backbone, that first opening becomes the anus, and the second becomes the mouth.

items.p: A tube gut holds 5 balls. One ball goes in every 2 counts. How long does each ball stay inside?
items.a: 10 counts
items.why: A ball leaves when five more pushes have happened. 5 pushes of 2 counts each make 10 counts.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Whale's flipper. Bat's wing. Mole's hand. Shark's fin.
items.a: Shark's fin. The other three hold arm and finger bones inherited from the same ancestors. A shark's fin has none.
items.why: The flipper, the wing and the hand are homologous. The shark's fin is only analogous to the flipper.

items.p: A swift and a swallow look alike. Explain how you would find out whether they are close relatives.
items.a: Compare the inside, part by part: the wing bones, the feet, the embryos and the DNA. Look for many detailed features that catching insects in the air does not explain.
items.why: A strong answer looks past shape and way of life, and names at least two kinds of inside evidence.

items.p: Ten wrists are tested and all ten show the cord. Explain why this does not prove everyone has one.
items.a: The cord is missing in only a small share of hands, so a group of ten can easily have none by chance. Many more people would have to be tested.
items.why: A strong answer says that a small group can miss something uncommon, and that a bigger survey is needed.

items.p: Draw a sac gut and a tube gut. Use arrows to show how food and waste move in each.
items.a: The sac has one opening, with arrows going in and coming back out the same way. The tube has arrows going in at the mouth and out at the anus.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one opening used twice in the sac, and one-way travel in the tube.

items.p: A python has two small spurs where the hind legs of her ancestors were.

views.says: The spurs are leftovers of legs. They show that the ancestors of pythons walked.
Pythons use the spurs in mating. So they are working parts, not leftovers.

items.ask: Can both be right? Say why or why not.
items.a: Both can be right. Vestigial means that a part has lost most of its old job, which was walking. Such a part can still keep or gain a smaller job.
items.why: A strong answer separates two questions: where the part came from, and what it does now.

items.p: A giraffe's voice-box nerve loops down to the chest and back up. What does this route show?
opts: The body is an older body, altered
The nerve grows longer every year
items.why: In a fish the matching nerve takes a direct path. As necks grew longer over generations, the nerve stayed looped round the same blood vessel. The detour is a sign of the older layout.

items.p: Which statement about a bat's wing and a crow's wing is correct?
opts: Homologous as limbs, analogous as wings
items.why: Both inherited the front limb with its bones, so the limbs are homologous. But flying arose separately in bats and birds, and the wings are built differently, so as wings they are analogous.

items.p: Why is DNA alone not enough to place most extinct animals in the family tree?
opts: Almost no fossil keeps any DNA
Bones are easier to read than DNA
items.why: DNA breaks down over time, so nearly all fossils are bone or shell with no DNA left. Extinct animals did have DNA while they lived.

items.p: A starfish is a closer relative of a human than of a jellyfish.
items.why: True. Starfish and humans both make the anus first as embryos, and DNA agrees. The ring shape of a starfish and of a jellyfish arose separately.

items.p: Animals of very different sizes can share one body plan.
items.why: True. A mouse and a blue whale are both chordates and both mammals. Size changes easily, and the body plan stays.

items.p: The firm, bendy rod along the back of a chordate embryo is the ____.
items.why: In animals with a backbone, the backbone forms round the notochord. What is left of the rod becomes part of the discs between the bones.

items.p: Each generation can only ____ the body that the parents passed on. Nothing starts from a blank sheet.
items.why: Bodies are inherited. So every body is an older body with changes, and it keeps signs of the older one.

items.p: Match each check for 'the same part' to the question it asks.
pairs: Is it in the same place, beside the same neighbours?
Is it built from the same pieces?
Does it form in the same way in the embryo?
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Parts that pass all three checks are very likely to be the same inherited part. Your arm and a bat's wing pass all three.

items.p: Sort each clue: does it show that two animals are relatives, or only that they live alike?
cats: Shows only that they live alike
items: the same bones in the same order
embryos built by the same steps
Shows only that they live alike
Shows only that they live alike
Shows only that they live alike
items.a: as given
items.why: Shape, home and armour can arise separately in animals who live in the same way. Bones, DNA and embryo steps are inherited.

items.p: Put these animals in order, from your most distant relative to your closest.
items.why: Each animal shares one more inherited feature with you than the one before: tissues, three layers, anus formed first, and a notochord and backbone.

items.p: About 4 in every 5 named animals are arthropods. Out of 100 named animals, about how many are not arthropods?
items.why: 4 in every 5 is the same as 80 in every 100. 100 take away 80 leaves 20. All the fish, birds, snails, worms and mammals fit into that 20.

items.p: Food and air cross paths in your throat, so people can choke. Explain how comparing bodies makes sense of this.
items.a: Lungs began as a pouch off the gut in fish ancestors. So the airway still branches off the food tube. The body was altered from an older one and was not planned afresh.
items.why: A strong answer says where lungs came from, and that an inherited layout can only be altered.

items.p: 'Animals who look alike must be relatives.' Give one example that shows why looking alike is not enough.
items.a: A dolphin and a shark look alike, but the dolphin has lungs, milk and arm bones, and is a relative of cows. Pangolins and armadillos both have armour, but are not close relatives.
items.why: A strong answer names two look-alikes and gives an inside feature that separates them.

items.p: Draw an embryo with three germ layers. Label each layer and write one body part that grows from it.
items.a: Outer layer: skin and nerves. Middle layer: muscle, bone and blood. Inner layer: the lining of the gut.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three sheets, one inside the other, each with a correct body part.

items.p: A prawn's nerve cord runs along the belly. A fish's nerve cord runs along the back.

views.says: An ancestor of the fish turned over. The two nerve cords are the same inherited part.
The shared ancestor had a loose net of nerves. Each group gathered it into a cord separately.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing? What evidence would help to decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and names evidence such as fossils of early ancestors, the genes that set back and belly, or animals whose nerves are still a loose net.
items.why: Both views accept the same facts about where the cords lie. They differ on whether the cords are one inherited part or two.

quiz.p: Which of these is a feature of an animal's body plan?
opts: Whether the gut has one opening or two
quiz.why: A body plan is the basic layout that is set in the embryo. Colour and speed can change quickly over generations, and the layout changes very little.

quiz.p: Ants, crabs and spiders are in one phylum. What do they all share?
opts: Jointed legs and a skeleton on the outside
A sac gut with one opening
quiz.why: They are arthropods. A backbone belongs to the chordate body plan, and a sac gut to jellyfish and flatworms.

quiz.p: Which feature does every chordate have at some stage of life?
opts: A notochord, a firm rod along the back
A hard skeleton on the outside
quiz.why: The notochord gives the chordates their name. You had one as an embryo. The other two answers describe arthropods.

quiz.p: A whale's flipper and a shark's fin look alike. Are they homologous parts?
opts: Yes. Both animals live in the sea
quiz.why: The flipper holds arm and finger bones, and the fin holds none. The two are analogous. Doing the same job in the same place does not make parts the same part.

quiz.p: Which is the best evidence that two animals are close relatives?
opts: Many matching parts inside the body
quiz.why: Shape and home can be shared by animals who simply live alike. Many detailed inside features that the way of life does not need are best explained by shared ancestors.

quiz.p: Why do some healthy people have no palmaris longus muscle in the forearm?
opts: The muscle has lost its main job
quiz.why: The muscle did more in ancestors who climbed. In humans it does very little. A part like that is not always built, and some people are born with none. Exercise and injury have nothing to do with whether a muscle is built.

quiz.p: If a survey of ten wrists finds the cord in every one, then no human lacks the cord.
quiz.why: False. Ten wrists is a small group, and a small group can easily miss something uncommon. Bigger studies find people with no cord.

quiz.p: Bones pointed to one ancestor for whales and DNA pointed to another. What did scientists do?
opts: Looked for more evidence, and found ankle bones
Chose the bones, because bones are older
quiz.why: When two kinds of evidence disagree, the answer is to find more. Ankle bones of early whales, found later, agreed with the DNA.

quiz.p: What do very young embryos of a fish, a chick and a human show?
opts: Each is a tiny copy of the adult
The human one has working gills
quiz.why: All three have throat folds and a tail. Embryos of relatives are built by inherited steps, and the earliest steps differ least. A human embryo never has gills.

quiz.p: Which sentence about animal bodies is correct?
opts: Each body is an older body, altered
Each body is planned fresh for its job
Bodies stay the same over generations
quiz.why: Every animal inherits a body and passes it on with small changes. That is why bodies keep leftover parts and odd routes, such as the long nerve in a giraffe's neck.

quiz.p: Why can each part of a tube gut do one job well?
opts: Food passes the parts in one order
Food moves both ways along it
quiz.why: Food moves one way in a tube, so grinding can come first and taking in can come later. In a sac, new food and old waste share one space.

applications: Surgeons repair a damaged tendon in the hand or the wrist with the palmaris longus tendon from the same person's forearm, because the hand works without it.
Medicines are tested on mice and other animals because their organs are homologous to human organs. The same reasoning warns that a mouse is not a small human.
Scientists who find a single fossil bone can often tell what kind of animal it came from, by comparing it with the bones of living animals.
Wildlife officers identify bones, teeth and scales seized from smugglers by comparing them with known skeletons, to find out which protected animal was killed.
Doctors who study how babies form use fish, chick and mouse embryos, because the early steps are shared.
Engineers who design flapping robots study bat wings and bird wings to see two different ways of building a wing from one kind of limb.
Vets use the same names for a dog's bones as doctors use for a human's, because the bones are the same bones.

open_questions.q: Did the tube gut, with a mouth and an anus, arise once or several times?
open_questions.why_open: The genes that build an anus differ a good deal between groups of animals. Some scientists read this as a sign that the second opening arose more than once. Others think it arose once and the genes changed later.

open_questions.q: Is an insect's nerve cord the same inherited part as your spinal cord?
open_questions.why_open: The genes that mark back and belly match in flies and frogs, on opposite sides. But the shared ancestor is unknown, and may have had only a loose net of nerves.

open_questions.q: Why do animals with four limbs have five fingers and not eight?
open_questions.why_open: Acanthostega, an early four-limbed animal who lived about 365 million years ago, had eight fingers on each hand. Nobody knows why five became the usual number in all the groups that came later.

open_questions.q: Do the small muscles round human ears still do anything?
open_questions.why_open: A study in 2020 found that these muscles become slightly active on the side a person is listening to. Whether that weak pull helps hearing at all has not been shown.

open_questions.q: What exactly makes two parts 'the same part'?
open_questions.why_open: Bones, embryos and genes usually agree about which parts match. Sometimes they do not: one gene can help to build parts that arose separately. Scientists and philosophers have no single agreed definition yet.

maths.problem: Kavya's family tested 16 wrists. 13 showed the cord, 2 showed none and 1 was not sure. What fraction of the wrists they were sure about had no cord?
maths.explain: 16 wrists take away the 1 not sure leaves 15. Of those 15, 2 had no cord. So the fraction is 2 out of 15, which is a little more than 1 in 8.
maths.context: In the Wrist Tendon Survey, you look at each wrist for a thin cord and write yes, no or not sure. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare your family with a much bigger study, even though the numbers of people are very different.

maths.problem: A study in Jabalpur tested 385 young adults. In 65 of them the cord was missing in one wrist, and in 13 it was missing in both. About how many people in a class of 30 would you expect to have a cord missing?
maths.explain: 65 and 13 make 78 people with a cord missing. 78 out of 385 is close to 80 out of 400, which is 1 in 5. One fifth of 30 is 6. A real class could have a few more or a few fewer.
maths.context: In the Wrist Tendon Survey you test a small group. Scientists in Jabalpur did the same wrist test on 385 people in 2010.
maths.why_maths: A proportion from a big study lets you predict what a smaller group is likely to show.

maths.problem: In one study in South India, the cord was missing in about 1 hand in every 15. Farhan's family tested 12 wrists and found the cord in all of them. Does this show that the study was wrong? Explain with numbers.
maths.answer: No. With 12 wrists you would expect fewer than 1 without a cord, so finding none is not surprising.
maths.explain: 1 in 15 means that 15 wrists would have about 1 missing, on average. 12 is fewer than 15, so the expected number is less than 1. A result of 0 fits well. Farhan would need a few hundred wrists to check the study.
maths.context: In the Wrist Tendon Survey, a small family may find no wrist without the cord. Farhan's family is made up. The study is real.
maths.why_maths: Working out the expected number tells you whether a result of zero is a surprise or just what a small group usually gives.

maths.problem: In a made-up run of Sac or Tube, the sock took 84 seconds for 12 balls with its best plan, and the tube took 36 seconds. About how many times as fast was the tube? How many balls a minute did the tube digest?
maths.answer: A little more than 2 times as fast. The tube digested 20 balls a minute.
maths.explain: 84 divided by 36 is 2 and a third. For the rate, 12 balls in 36 seconds is 1 ball every 3 seconds. A minute has 60 seconds, and 60 divided by 3 is 20.
maths.context: In Sac or Tube you time how long a sock and a paper tube take to 'digest' twelve paper balls.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other shows how big the difference is, and a rate lets you compare guts that were given different amounts of food.

maths.problem: One hand has 8 wrist bones, 5 palm bones and 14 finger and thumb bones. One foot has 7 ankle bones, 5 sole bones and 14 toe bones. A grown-up has 206 bones. Are more than half of them in the hands and feet?
maths.answer: Yes. The two hands and two feet hold 106 bones, and half of 206 is 103.
maths.explain: One hand has 8 and 5 and 14, which is 27. One foot has 7 and 5 and 14, which is 26. Two hands make 54 and two feet make 52. 54 and 52 make 106. Half of 206 is 103, and 106 is more than that.
maths.context: In Your Leg Is a Second Arm, you count the bones of your hand and your foot and find the same pattern in both.
maths.why_maths: Adding the bones up shows how much of a skeleton is made of one repeated pattern, used four times.

maths.problem: About 1,500,000 kinds of animals have been named. About 1,257,000 of them are arthropods. Roughly what fraction is that? If you picked one named kind without looking, would you more likely pick an arthropod or a chordate?
maths.answer: About four fifths. You would much more likely pick an arthropod.
maths.explain: 1,257,000 is close to 1,200,000. 1,200,000 out of 1,500,000 is the same as 12 out of 15, which is 4 out of 5. Chordates are only about 70,000 kinds, which is less than 1 in 20.
maths.context: In Nested Boxes you sort one animal from each of the nine biggest groups. The groups are very unequal in size.
maths.why_maths: Rounding big numbers and turning them into a fraction shows at a glance which body plan most animals have.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how people found out who the whale's relatives are. It took more than three hundred years, and the last clue came from rocks in Kashmir.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time people counted whales as fish, because whales live in the sea and have fins. In 1680 the English doctor Edward Tyson cut open a porpoise in London. He found a folded brain like the brains of four-legged land animals, and he placed the porpoise with them. In 1758 Carl Linnaeus moved whales into the mammals. But which mammals were their relatives? Early whale fossils had teeth like those of an extinct group of wolf-like, hoofed meat-eaters. So in 1966 Leigh Van Valen proposed that group as the ancestors. Later, DNA studies disagreed. They put whales next to hippos, among the even-toed hoofed animals such as cows and deer. In 2001 two teams found early whales with legs in Pakistan. Their ankle bones had a double-pulley shape that only even-toed hoofed animals have. In 2007 a team led by Hans Thewissen, with Sunil Bajpai, studied Indohyus, a fox-sized fossil animal from Kashmir. The skull had a thick ear bone otherwise known only from whales. The Indian geologist A. Ranga Rao had collected those rocks years before, and his widow gave them to the scientists.
how_we_found_out.who: Edward Tyson, Carl Linnaeus, Philip Gingerich, Hans Thewissen, Sunil Bajpai and A. Ranga Rao
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: First, that whales are fish, because of their shape and their home. Tyson's dissection in 1680 showed a mammal's body inside. Second, that whales came from wolf-like meat-eaters, judged from teeth alone. Ankle bones found in 2001 and an ear bone described in 2007 showed that whales belong with the even-toed hoofed animals, as the DNA had said.
how_we_found_out.art: A small fox-sized, long-tailed, deer-like animal wading at the edge of a river, with a faint outline of a whale in the water behind.
